plot_variable_difference() displays the change in a variable between two saved time steps in 3D, calculated as time_b - time_a.

The color scale is centered symmetrically around zero to distinguish increases and decreases.

The relevant parameters are:

  • sim: The SimulationResults object.
  • var_name: Name of the point-data variable.
  • time_a (optional, default: None): First time step. Defaults to the first saved time step.
  • time_b (optional, default: None): Second time step. Defaults to the last saved time step.
  • cmap (default: "RdBu_r"): Colormap for the difference.
  • show_edges (default: False): Controls mesh edge visibility.
  • scale (default: (1, 1, 1)): Scaling factors for the X, Y, and Z directions.

Example call in the codebase:

plot_variable_difference(
    simulation_result,
    var_name="T",
    time_a=initial_time,
    time_b=final_time,
    cmap="RdBu_r",
    show_edges=False,
)

docs.title: Plot a cross-section difference
docs.text:
plot_cross_section_difference_2D() visualizes the change in a point-data variable between two time steps on a specified 2D plane. The difference is calculated as time_b - time_a.

The relevant parameters are:

  • sim: The SimulationResults object.
  • var_name: Name of the point-data variable.
  • time_a (optional, default: None): First time step.
  • time_b (optional, default: None): Second time step.
  • origin (default: (0, 0, 0)): Point on the section plane.
  • normal (default: (1, 0, 0)): Normal vector of the plane.
  • cmap (default: "RdBu_r"): Difference colormap.
  • n_contours (default: 15): Number of contour levels.
  • resolution (default: 200): Resolution of the interpolated 2D grid.

Example call in the codebase:

plot_cross_section_difference_2D(
    simulation_result,
    var_name="T",
    time_a=initial_time,
    time_b=final_time,
    origin=(500, 500, 500),
    normal=(0, 1, 0),
    cmap="RdBu_r",
)

docs.title: Print a variable at a point
docs.text:
print_variable_at_point() samples a result variable at a specified spatial point and time step.

The relevant parameters are:

  • sim: The SimulationResults object.
  • var_name: Variable to sample.
  • time: Time step used for sampling.
  • point: Spatial coordinates (x, y, z).

Example call in the codebase:

value = print_variable_at_point(
    simulation_result,
    var_name="T",
    time=final_time,
    point=(500, 500, 500),
)

print(value)

docs.title: Output structure
docs.text:
Both solver pipelines converge to the same WBGeo result type:

SfePy:
Build SfePy Hydrothermal Problem ─────┐
                                      ├─> Run SfePy Simulation ─┐
Build SfePy Custom Problem ───────────┘                         │
                                                                ├─> SimulationResults
GOLEM:                                                          │        │
Build GOLEM Hydrothermal Problem ─────┐                         │        ├─> Visualisation / Inspection
Build GOLEM Simple Reservoir Problem ─┼─> Run GOLEM Simulation ─┘        └─> Export Simulation Results
Build GOLEM Custom Problem ───────────┘

SimulationResults is a time-dependent container for geometry, topology, and numerical fields. It includes:

  • nodes_by_time --- nodal coordinates for each saved time step.
  • cells_by_time --- cell connectivity.
  • celltypes_by_time --- VTK-style cell type identifiers.
  • node_data_by_time --- node-based result variables.
  • cell_data_by_time --- cell-based result variables.
  • solver --- "sfepy" or "golem".
  • solver_output --- the solver's console output per stage.
  • solver_tables --- tabular solver output per file and column, e.g. GOLEM's postprocessor CSVs.
  • input_files --- the input file(s) the solver ran.
  • block_names --- the name of each element block, by block id.

Arrays that do not change between time steps, such as the geometry of an unchanged mesh, block ids (mat_id, ObjectId) or a steady-state field, are stored only once and shared by all time steps. A stored result therefore grows only with the fields that actually change.

docs.title: Structural Modeling
docs.text: The structural modeling component reconstructs 3D geological structure from sparse field observations. Structural modeling in general can be approached in many ways; this Workbench uses implicit methods, where the geometry is represented as the isosurfaces of a continuously interpolated scalar field rather than as explicit surfaces built by hand. The scalar field is fitted to surface contact points and (optionally) orientation measurements, and the result is a volumetric lithology model together with surface meshes that represent the boundaries between lithological units.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Surface points are locations where a geological interface has been observed — e.g. a formation contact in a borehole, an outcrop pick, or a digitised section. Each point carries an X, Y, Z coordinate and the name of the formation it belongs to. In the implicit framework used here, surface points define the base of the named geological element: the scalar field is fitted so that the isovalue for a given formation passes through its surface points from below.

Orientations are dip/azimuth measurements at known locations, represented as a gradient vector (G_x, G_y, G_z). They are optional, but some interpolation methods require them to produce a result while others do not consider them at all — see the interpolation methods table for details.

Stratigraphic groups organise formations into an unconformity-bounded sequence. Each group is interpolated independently, and groups are ordered youngest to oldest. Within a group, formations are also listed youngest to oldest — this ordering is used when assembling the final lithology block.

The mapping is a dictionary that assigns formations to groups:

{
  "Strat_Series2": ["rock3", "rock2"],
  "Strat_Series1": ["rock1", "basement"]
}

The key is the group name; the list contains the formations in that group, youngest first.

The grid is where the scalar fields are evaluated and the lithology is assigned. Two grids are available and can be used interchangeably for the fault and the structural model:

  • A Regular Grid divides the domain into voxels of equal size. Surfaces are extracted with marching cubes.
  • An Octree Grid starts from coarse blocks and refines them only where a surface or fault passes through, so the cells are fine near contacts and faults and coarse elsewhere. Surfaces are extracted with dual contouring. At its finest level, an Octree Grid gives the same model as a Regular Grid of the same resolution, with fewer cells.

All interpolation methods, fault modeling, unconformities and surface mesh types work on both grids.

docs.title: 1. Define the grid
docs.text:
Workbench components: Regular Grid or Octree Grid

Either grid can be connected to Compute Fault Model and Compute Structural Model. When a fault model is used, the fault model and the structural model must be computed on the same grid.

docs.title: Regular Grid
docs.text:
A RegularGrid defines the 3D computation domain as a regular axis-aligned voxel grid:

  • Extent — bounding box (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) in world coordinates. Should cover all input data with a small margin.
  • Resolution — number of voxels (nx, ny, nz). Higher resolution gives more geometric detail but increases computation time significantly.

docs.title: Octree Grid
docs.text:
An OctreeGrid defines the same kind of domain, but with cells of different sizes. The extent is first divided into base blocks, the coarsest cells of the grid. During modeling, a block is halved along every axis wherever a surface or fault passes through it, and again inside the halves, up to the maximum level. Cells that lie entirely within one formation stay coarse.

  • Extent — bounding box (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax), as for the Regular Grid.
  • Base resolution — number of base blocks (bx, by, bz). Choose them so that the blocks are close to cubic, e.g. (10, 4, 4) for an extent of 2500 × 1000 × 1000.
  • Max level — how many times a base block can be halved. The finest cells have the size of a base block divided by 2**max_level, so the finest resolution is base_resolution * 2**max_level (e.g. (10, 4, 4) at level 4 gives 160 × 64 × 64). Level 0 gives a plain regular grid of base blocks.
  • Gap mitigation (optional) — where a surface crosses cells of different sizes, dual contouring can leave small gaps. balance_mesh_depth_adjacency (default) refines the cells next to the finest ones as well, which closes these gaps at the cost of extra cells. none skips this step.
  • Cell balance (optional) — none (default) lets a finest cell sit next to a much coarser one. face_2to1 adds cells so that cells sharing a face differ by at most one level, for a more gradual transition between fine and coarse cells.
from core.structural_modeling_components.structural_objects.grids.grid_classes import OctreeGrid

grid = OctreeGrid(extent=(0, 2500, 0, 1000, 0, 1000), base_resolution=(10, 4, 4), max_level=4)

The rest of the workflow is the same as with a Regular Grid.

docs.title: 2. Load input data
docs.text:
Workbench component: Structural Input Data

Surface points are required. Orientations are optional — whether they are needed depends on the interpolation method chosen later (see the interpolation methods table). The mapping described above is provided as a Python dictionary or configured directly in the visual interface (visual DSL). Together they form the InputData_StructuralElements object that feeds the model.

The required columns are: - Surface points: X, Y, Z, formation - Orientations (if provided): X, Y, Z, G_x, G_y, G_z, formation

docs.title: 3. (Optional) Build the fault model
docs.text:
Workbench components: Fault Input Data → Compute Fault Model

If the geological model includes faults, they must be modelled before the stratigraphic interpolation. The fault workflow is:

  1. Load fault surface points and orientations into InputData_FaultElements.
  2. Call build_fault_frame to create the FaultFrame.
  3. Call compute_fault_domains to interpolate each fault scalar field and partition the grid into fault domains. This step also extracts fault surface meshes.

Fault interpolation uses Universal Co-Kriging exclusively, so both surface points and orientations are required for every fault. Orientation vectors are scaled to unit length first, so only their direction matters. The result is a FaultModelResults object containing:

  • A surface mesh for each fault (the boundary between hanging wall and footwall).
  • A domain map that partitions every cell of the grid (voxel or octree cell) into strictly separate, non-overlapping fault blocks. Stratigraphic groups that are active for a given fault will be interpolated independently in each of its domains; groups that post-date the fault are not affected by the domain split. The domain map is only computed if no faults cross-cut (see limitations below).

Limitations of the fault model:

  • Cross-cutting faults are not supported for structural modeling. Each pair of faults is tested for isovalue-band overlap after interpolation. If two fault surfaces intersect within the model domain, the fault model is still computed and can be inspected (the 3D plot highlights the line where the faults cross), but the result is flagged cross_cutting=True, has no domain map, and is rejected by Compute Structural Model / build_structural_frame with an error. Fix the fault geometry and recompute the fault model.
  • Every fault must split the grid. A fault whose scalar field does not actually separate the domain into two non-empty sides will raise an error. Faults that are entirely outside the grid extent, or whose surface does not reach across the domain, cannot be modelled.

docs.title: 4. Build the structural model
docs.text:
Workbench component: Compute Structural Model

This step combines configuration and computation. The input data, grid, and — optionally — the fault model are assembled into a StructuralFrame. The following configuration options are available before running the computation:

  • Interpolation method per group (optional) — defaults to Radial Basis Function. Set per group with frame["GroupName"].set_interpolation_method("Universal Co-Kriging").
  • Interpolation parameters (optional) — default values are estimated from the input data. Override with frame["GroupName"].configure_interpolation_params(nelements=20000).
  • Fault activity (only relevant when a fault model is attached) — controls which stratigraphic groups are offset by each fault. frame.set_fault_activity_by_group(fault_name="Fault-1", group_name="Strat_Series2") marks the specified group as the youngest one affected. Groups older than or equal to it are interpolated separately in each fault domain; groups younger than it are treated as post-fault and interpolated across the full grid.

The computation runs the following steps in sequence:

  1. Validation — checks that every active fault domain contains sufficient input data for the chosen interpolation method in each group (for example, that orientation data is present in each domain for methods that require it, or that there are enough surface points for the chosen method). The same check runs in the Workbench as a pre-check when the inputs are connected. All issues are reported together before any expensive computation begins.
  2. Interpolation — each stratigraphic group is interpolated independently. When faults are active for a group, the interpolation is run completely separately in each fault domain using only the data points that fall within that domain. The resulting scalar fields are then stitched together.
  3. Age masks — a boolean mask is computed per group that represents its depositional extent: the oldest group underlies the entire domain (mask is True everywhere), while younger groups are only present where they were deposited. When assembling the lithology block, younger groups take precedence over older ones wherever their mask is True — this is what produces unconformable contacts between groups.
  4. Lithology block — the scalar fields and age masks are combined into a single integer array where each cell is assigned to a formation.
  5. Surface meshes — isosurfaces are extracted from the scalar fields using marching cubes on a Regular Grid, or dual contouring on an Octree Grid. Five mesh types are stored per element: masked (respects unconformities and fault domains), unmasked (full isosurface through the entire grid), combined (derived from the lithology block), extended (extrapolated beyond the grid boundary, used as input for 3D mesh generation), and extended_masked (extrapolated beyond the grid boundary like extended, but one separate piece per fault domain, cut at the faults and at the base of younger groups; see Output).

Limitations of the structural model:

  • Group interactions are limited to unconformities. The only geometric relationship supported between stratigraphic groups is that a younger group erodes the top of an older one. There is no support for intrusions, cross-cutting bodies, or any other non-erosional contact geometry between groups.
  • Sufficient data required in every active fault domain. When a fault is active for a group, the interpolation in each fault domain uses only the data points that fall within that domain. The validation step rejects domains with too few surface points for the chosen method, or without orientations for methods that need them (UCK, FDI, PLI, GeoINR); the minimum for each method is given in its section below. A domain without any surface points of a group is skipped: the group is not interpolated there. Even above the minimum, sparse data in a domain gives a less reliable result.

docs.title: Interpolation Methods
docs.text:
All methods produce the same output format (scalar field + per-element isovalues) and can be set per stratigraphic group. The exposed parameters listed below are a subset of the full configuration space — each underlying library (SciPy, PyKrige, GemPy, LoopStructural, PyTorch) has many additional options that are not exposed.

Method Orientations required Library Adjustable parameters Radial Basis Function (RBF) No SciPy kernel, smoothing, epsilon, neighbors, anisotropy_scaling_z (see below) Ordinary Kriging (OK) No PyKrige variogram_model, range, nugget, anisotropy_scaling_y/z, neighbors (see below) Universal Kriging (UK) No PyKrige Same as OK without neighbors (see below) Universal Co-Kriging (UCK) Yes GemPy None (see below) Finite Differences (FDI) Yes LoopStructural nelements, regularisation, orientation_weight (see below) Piecewise Linear (PLI) Yes LoopStructural nelements, regularisation, orientation_weight (see below) GeoINR Yes GeoINR (custom) orientation_weight, hidden_dim, n_hidden_layers, epochs, lr, seed (see below)

For all methods that use orientations, only the direction of the orientation vectors affects the result, not their length: UCK normalises them before passing them to GemPy, LoopStructural normalises them for FDI and PLI, and GeoINR normalises them in its orientation loss. Orientations can lie anywhere, not only on an interface; their formation only assigns them to a group.

Two of these parameters take one of a fixed set of options. An unknown option is rejected when it is set.

Parameter Methods Options (default first) kernel RBF thin_plate_spline, linear, cubic, quintic, multiquadric, inverse_multiquadric, inverse_quadratic, gaussian variogram_model OK, UK gaussian, spherical, exponential, hole-effect

Default parameters are estimated automatically from the spatial distribution of the input points (data scale, point count, nearest-neighbour distance) and can be overridden via configure_interpolation_params. The estimate uses all points of a group, across all fault domains. Parameter choice has a large influence on the resulting model — the default values are a reasonable starting point but should be treated as a first guess rather than an optimal configuration. In particular, variogram range and anisotropy for kriging methods, regularisation for FDI and PLI (and nelements for PLI with little data), and the number of epochs and network capacity for GeoINR can all significantly change the shape and smoothness of the interpolated surfaces.

docs.title: Radial Basis Function (RBF)
docs.text:
RBF fits a smooth scalar field through the surface points of a group: each formation gets a value (oldest = 1, youngest = n), and the field between the points is built from one radial function per point plus, for some kernels, a polynomial trend. Orientations are not used; if they are given, a warning says so. RBF is the default method.

A group with only one formation. RBF needs at least two formations to tell up from down. For a group with a single formation, a copy of its surface points is placed below them (shifted down by 10 % of the point cloud's diagonal) as an artificial older formation, and a warning is shown. This assumes roughly horizontal layers; for steep or overturned layers, use a method with orientations (UCK, FDI, PLI, GeoINR).

Minimum data. The kernels thin_plate_spline, cubic and quintic add a polynomial trend, which has to be fitted from the points. They need a minimum number of surface points in each group and fault domain, and the points must not all lie in one plane (for example, a single flat surface on its own). The copied points of a single-formation group count. The other kernels work with a single point.

Kernel Trend Minimum surface points thin_plate_spline (default), cubic plane 4, not all in one plane quintic curved surface 10, not all on one plane or one simple curved surface linear, multiquadric, gaussian, inverse_multiquadric, inverse_quadratic none or constant 1

This is checked before the computation (and in the Workbench when the inputs are connected). If a group or fault domain has too few points, add points there or choose linear or multiquadric.

Parameter Meaning Default Effect kernel Shape of the radial function thin_plate_spline thin_plate_spline gives smooth, gently extrapolating surfaces and needs no length scale. Kernels using epsilon are more local. smoothing How far the field may deviate from the points (0 = passes exactly through them) 0.05 Larger values give smoother surfaces that no longer honour every point; useful for noisy data. The scale is the step between two formations (1). epsilon Shape parameter, an inverse length (only multiquadric, inverse_multiquadric, inverse_quadratic, gaussian; ignored by the others) 1 / (5 × median nearest-neighbour distance) Larger values make each point's influence more local. Refers to the stretched coordinates when anisotropy_scaling_z is not 1. neighbors Number of nearest points used at each grid cell (empty = all points) all points; for more than 5000 points min(500, 5 · n^(2/3)) Fewer neighbours are faster and more local, but can produce small steps in the surfaces. Must be at least 4 (10 for quintic). anisotropy_scaling_z Vertical stretching factor applied to points and grid before fitting 1.0 (no anisotropy) Values above 1 make vertical distances count more than horizontal ones, so points influence each other more along the layers than across them. Values below 1 do the opposite.

docs.title: Ordinary Kriging (OK)
docs.text:
Ordinary Kriging interpolates the scalar field from the surface points with a variogram, which describes how quickly two points become independent with increasing distance. Each formation gets a value (oldest = 1, youngest = n), as for RBF. Orientations are not used; if they are given, a warning says so. A group with only one formation gets the same copied formation below it as described for RBF.

Minimum data. At least 2 surface points in each group and fault domain (the copied points of a single-formation group count). This is checked before the computation.

The defaults are derived from the spread of the points: per axis, the distance between the 10 % and 90 % quantiles of the point coordinates.

Parameter Meaning Default Effect variogram_model Shape of the variogram: gaussian, spherical, exponential, hole-effect gaussian gaussian gives the smoothest surfaces. spherical and exponential give slight kinks at the points. hole-effect is meant for periodic structures. range Distance (model units) up to which points influence each other 20 × median nearest-neighbour distance, limited to between 0.1 × the largest spread and 1.5 × the diagonal of the spread Longer ranges give smoother, more regional surfaces; shorter ranges follow the points more locally. nugget Fraction of the variance that is not spatially correlated (0 to below 1) 0 0 = surfaces pass exactly through the points. Larger values give smoother surfaces that no longer honour every point; useful for noisy data. anisotropy_scaling_y Factor applied to y coordinates before kriging, relative to x spread in y / spread in x, limited to 0.05–1 Values below 1 make distances along y count less, i.e. a longer range along y. anisotropy_scaling_z Factor applied to z coordinates before kriging, relative to x spread in z / spread in x, limited to 0.05–1 Values below 1 make vertical distances count less, i.e. a longer vertical range. For layered data the vertical spread is small, so the default reproduces the gradual vertical change between layers smoothly. neighbors Number of nearest points used at each grid cell (moving window; empty = all points) all points below 20 points; otherwise n / 10, limited to 30–200 A moving window keeps memory low for many points but is slower. If a fault domain has no more points than neighbors, all its points are used.

The sill (the total variance) is fixed at 1, because it does not change the interpolated field; only the nugget relative to it does. A tiny nugget (10⁻⁶ of the sill) is always added internally to keep the computation numerically stable, which is most important for the Gaussian variogram. It does not visibly change the result.

docs.title: Universal Kriging (UK)
docs.text:
Universal Kriging works like Ordinary Kriging, but additionally fits a linear trend (a + b·x + c·y + d·z) together with the variogram. This suits dipping layers whose scalar field changes steadily across the model. Orientations are not used, and a single-formation group gets the copied formation as for RBF. Universal Kriging always uses all points (there is no moving window), so memory grows with the number of points and grid cells.

Minimum data. At least 4 surface points in each group and fault domain, not all in one plane (for example, a single flat surface on its own). Otherwise the linear trend cannot be fitted. If a domain has too few points, add points there or use Ordinary Kriging.

The parameters are the same as for Ordinary Kriging, without neighbors, and the internal jitter is added in the same way. Two defaults differ:

Parameter Default range 30 × median nearest-neighbour distance, limited to between 0.15 × and 0.9 × the largest spread anisotropy_scaling_y, anisotropy_scaling_z spread in y (z) / spread in x, limited to 0.05–20

docs.title: Universal Co-Kriging (UCK)
docs.text:
Universal Co-Kriging (implemented with GemPy) interpolates the scalar field from surface points and orientations together: the surface points of each formation define where its surface lies, the orientations define the dip direction of the layers. Only the direction of the orientation vectors matters; they are scaled to unit length before use. Because the orientations define which way is up, a group with a single formation works without the copied formation used by RBF and Kriging. After the interpolation, the scalar field is rescaled so that the formations get the values 1 … n like in the other methods.

UCK has no adjustable parameters: GemPy's default settings are used, which are derived from the model extent.

Minimum data. In each group and fault domain:

  • at least one orientation, and
  • at least one surface point of every formation of the group. UCK takes each formation's value from that formation's own points, so a formation without points in a fault domain cannot be placed there. The other methods number the formations from the group order and do not need this.

Both are checked before the computation. If a formation is missing in a fault domain, add surface points of it there, or use another method for this group.

docs.title: Finite Differences (FDI) and Piecewise Linear (PLI)
docs.text:
FDI and PLI (both implemented with LoopStructural) solve the scalar field on their own internal computation grid, which covers the model extent plus a 20 % margin. FDI uses a regular grid of cells, PLI a mesh of tetrahedra. Each formation gets a value (oldest = 1, youngest = n), as for RBF. The field is the weighted least-squares solution of three conditions:

  • it has the formation's value at every surface point (weight 1);
  • its layers have the measured dip at every orientation (weight orientation_weight);
  • it is smooth (weight regularisation).

Only the ratios between these weights matter. Orientations set only the dip at their location; they do not pull an interface towards them, so they can lie anywhere, for example in the middle of a layer. If a group (or a fault domain) has surface points of only one formation, LoopStructural uses the orientations to define which way is up, so a group with a single formation works without the copied formation used by RBF and Kriging.

LoopStructural's piecewise-linear interpolator has no gradient constraint. For PLI, each orientation is therefore passed as two tangent constraints: the field's gradient must be perpendicular to the strike vector and to the dip vector, which is equivalent to a gradient constraint without its length. LoopStructural weights tangent constraints by the volume of their mesh element; the weight passed to it is divided by the mean element volume, so orientation_weight has the same effect for any nelements.

Minimum data. At least one orientation in each group and fault domain that contains surface points. This is checked before the computation.

Parameter Methods Meaning Default Effect nelements FDI, PLI Number of elements of the internal computation grid (at least 1000) FDI: 10 000 × √(points / 1000), limited to 5000–200 000; PLI: 2000 × √(points / 1000) × 0.8–1.4 (denser sampling of the model gives the larger factor), limited to 2000–50 000 More elements give finer surfaces but take much longer; beyond the default, the result usually changes only slightly. For small or sparse data, PLI's default mesh can be too coarse to follow the orientations; increase nelements (e.g. to 10 000) if the layers do not follow the measured dips. regularisation FDI, PLI Weight of the smoothness term 0.1 Larger values give smoother, more planar surfaces that may not honour every data point; smaller values follow the data more closely but can become wavy. LoopStructural's own default for FDI (1.0) gives noticeably smoother surfaces that follow the data less closely. orientation_weight FDI, PLI Weight of the orientations relative to the surface points 1.0 Larger values make the layers follow the measured dips more closely; smaller values let the surfaces follow the surface points more closely. Matters most when there are few surface points.

The solver (conjugate gradients with LoopStructural's default tolerance) is fixed.

docs.title: GeoINR
docs.text:
GeoINR represents the scalar field by a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron, implicit neural representation) that returns the field value for any location; the implementation follows the GeoINR reference implementation. Each formation gets a fixed label, evenly spaced from +1 (youngest) to −1 (oldest). The network is trained by minimising three terms:

  • the difference between the field and the formation's label at every surface point;
  • the angle between the field's gradient and the measured orientation at every orientation (weight orientation_weight);
  • the deviation of the gradient magnitude across the model from the gradient magnitude at the surface points (fixed weight). This keeps the field from folding back far away from the data.

Coordinates are scaled by the same factor on all axes, so the measured dips are not distorted. As for FDI and PLI, orientations set only the dip and can lie anywhere, and a group with a single formation works without a copied formation, because the orientations define which way is up.

Randomness. Training starts from random network weights, so the result depends on the random start, more so the sparser the data. seed fixes the start: the same input and seed give the same model. To judge how robust a model is, compute it with a few different seeds; if the results differ strongly, add data or try a smaller learning rate.

Runtime. The network is trained separately for each group and fault domain, which takes from seconds to minutes per group on a CPU. A CUDA-capable GPU is used automatically if PyTorch finds one.

Minimum data. At least one orientation in each group and fault domain that contains surface points. This is checked before the computation. Formations without surface points in a fault domain still get their label there.

The defaults depend on the number of surface points of the group (n).

Parameter Meaning Default Effect orientation_weight Weight of the orientations relative to the surface points 0.3 Larger values make the layers follow the measured dips more closely; smaller values let the surfaces follow the surface points more closely. If the dip is known mainly from orientations, increase it; if orientations disagree with the surface points, decrease it. hidden_dim Number of neurons per hidden layer 32; 64 from 3000 points More neurons can represent more complex geometry (e.g. tight folds) but train more slowly and may overfit sparse data. n_hidden_layers Number of hidden layers 2 Fewer layers give a less flexible field; 1 to 3 is usually enough. epochs Number of training steps 4000; 2500 from 5000 points More steps can fit the data better but take longer. lr Learning rate (step size of the training) 0.01; 0.005 from 800 points; 0.003 from 5000 points Smaller values train more steadily but need more steps. seed Start value of the random number generator 0 Changes the random start of the training (see above).

Fixed (not adjustable): Softplus activation, the weight of the gradient-magnitude term (0.05, evaluated at 2000 randomly chosen grid points), and the AdamW optimiser with a learning rate decaying to zero over the training. The network weights of the training step with the lowest loss are used.

docs.title: Visualisation and Inspection
docs.text:
Workbench: Where available, these are exposed as inspector functions with limited functionality in the visual interface (visual DSL) — only some parameters can be set there (noted per function); the codebase functions below expose the full set of options.

The following components allow quick inspection of input data and model results without leaving the Workbench.

docs.title: Preview raw input data
docs.text:
Workbench components: Plot Input Data 3D, Plot Fault Input Data 3D

Before running the model, surface points and orientations can be previewed directly — no StructuralFrame required.

  • plot_input_data_3D(input_data) — 3D plot of structural surface points and orientations, colored by formation.
    • input_data: An InputData_StructuralElements object.
    • show_orientations (optional): If True, draws orientation arrows. Default True.
    • arrow_scale (optional): Length of the orientation arrows. Defaults to 5% of the data's bounding box diagonal.
    • point_size (optional): Size of the surface point markers. Default 8.
    • notebook (optional): Use PyVista's notebook rendering mode. Default False.
    • show (optional): If True, opens the interactive window immediately. Default True.
  • plot_fault_input_data_3D(input_data) — the same, for fault input data (InputData_FaultElements), colored by fault name instead of formation. Same parameters as above.
plot_input_data_3D(data_structural_elements)
plot_fault_input_data_3D(data_faults)

docs.title: Inspect the structural model
docs.text:
Workbench components: Detailed Report, Plot Model Result 2D, Plot Model Result 3D

These act on a StructuralModelResults object (see Output below).

Detailed Report prints a text summary of the structural frame — grid, group count, surface point and orientation counts, and per-group interpolation method and parameters. On an Octree Grid, it also lists the grid settings and, once the model is computed, the number of cells per level and their share of the finest cells:

structural_model_result.structural_frame.detailed_report()

Plot Model Result 3D — plot_structural_model_3D(frame, ...):

  • frame: The StructuralFrame to visualise, e.g. structural_model_result.structural_frame.
  • mesh_type (optional): Which geological surface mesh to render — "masked", "unmasked", "combined", "extended", or "extended_masked" (see Output). Default "masked".
  • fault_mesh_type (optional): Mesh type for fault surfaces. Defaults to mesh_type if not set.
  • show_surface_meshes (optional): Render the per-element surface meshes. Default True.
  • show_points (optional): Render input surface points. Default True.
  • show_orientations (optional): Render orientation arrows. Default True.
  • fault_opacity (optional): Opacity of fault surface meshes. Default 0.35.
  • show_lith_block (optional): Show the lithology block as the outside of the model — the cells on the six walls of the extent, colored by formation and with their edges drawn, so the grid's cells (uniform voxels, or octree cells of different sizes) are visible. The block hides what lies inside it. Default False.
  • notebook (optional): Use PyVista's notebook rendering mode. Default False.
  • off_screen (optional): Render off-screen with no window — required before calling .screenshot() without show(). Default False.
  • show (optional): If True, opens the interactive window immediately; set False to add further actors before displaying. Default True.

The Workbench version exposes mesh_type as a drop-down (default "masked"); faults use the same type where it exists, otherwise "unmasked". The other options keep their defaults.

plot_structural_model_3D(structural_model_result.structural_frame, mesh_type="masked", fault_opacity=0.5)

Plot Model Result 2D — plot_structural_model_2D(frame, ...):

  • frame: The StructuralFrame to visualise.
  • axis (optional): Axis to slice along — "x", "y", or "z". Default "y".
  • index (optional): Slice index along the chosen axis, counted in the finest cells on an Octree Grid. Defaults to the mid-point.
  • show_result (optional): Overlay the lithology block as a colored background. Default True.
  • show_fault_contours (optional): Overlay fault isolines. Default True.
  • show_input_data (optional): Overlay input surface points and orientation arrows. Default True.
  • show_grid (optional): Outline the grid cells the slice cuts — uniform voxels on a Regular Grid, cells of different sizes on an Octree Grid. Default False.
  • title_suffix (optional): Text appended to the plot title. Default "".

The Workbench version exposes axis (a choice of x, y or z), index (empty = the mid-point) and show_grid; the other options keep their defaults.

plot_structural_model_2D(structural_model_result.structural_frame, axis="x", index=20)

docs.title: Inspect the fault model
docs.text:
Workbench components: Detailed Fault Report, Plot Fault Model Result 2D, Plot Fault Model Result 3D

These act on a FaultModelResults object.

Detailed Fault Report:

fault_model_result.fault_frame.detailed_report()

Plot Fault Model Result 3D — plot_fault_model_3D(fault_frame, ...):

  • fault_frame: The FaultFrame to visualise, e.g. fault_model_result.fault_frame.
  • mesh_type (optional): Which fault surface mesh to render — "masked", "unmasked", "extended", or "extended_masked" (see Output). Default "unmasked".
  • show_surface_meshes (optional): Render fault surface meshes. Default True.
  • show_input_data (optional): Render input surface points and orientation arrows. Default True.
  • show_domain_map (optional): Render translucent fault domain blocks. Default True.
  • domain_opacity (optional): Opacity of the domain blocks. Default 0.15.
  • highlight_crosscuts (optional): Highlight the line where two fault surfaces cross. Has no effect if no faults cross or if show_surface_meshes is False. Default True.
  • crosscut_color (optional): Color of the highlighted crosscut lines. Default "red".
  • crosscut_line_width (optional): Line width of the highlighted crosscut lines. Default 6.0.
  • notebook (optional): Use PyVista's notebook rendering mode. Default False.
  • show (optional): If True, opens the interactive window immediately. Default True.

The Workbench version exposes mesh_type as a drop-down (default "unmasked"); the other options keep their defaults.

plot_fault_model_3D(fault_model_result.fault_frame, show_domain_map=True, domain_opacity=0.2)

Plot Fault Model Result 2D — plot_fault_model_2D(fault_frame, ...):

  • fault_frame: The FaultFrame to visualise.
  • axis (optional): Axis to slice along — "x", "y", or "z". Default "y".
  • index (optional): Slice index along the chosen axis, counted in the finest cells on an Octree Grid. Defaults to the mid-point.
  • show_results (optional): Plot the fault domain map and isolines, if present. Default True.
  • show_input_data (optional): Plot input surface points, if available. Default True.
  • show_fault_contours (optional): Overlay fault isolines. Default True.
  • show_grid (optional): Outline the grid cells the slice cuts, as in plot_structural_model_2D. Default False.

The Workbench version exposes axis (a choice of x, y or z), index (empty = the mid-point) and show_grid, as in Plot Model Result 2D.

plot_fault_model_2D(fault_model_result.fault_frame, axis="y", index=15)

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Workbench: The structural_model output port of Compute Structural Model carries the result. It can be connected directly to meshing components or inspected in-place using Detailed Report, Plot Model Result 2D, and Plot Model Result 3D.

compute_structural_model returns a StructuralModelResults object containing a deep copy of the structural frame with all computed results attached:

  • Scalar fields — one float array per stratigraphic group, shaped (nx, ny, nz) on a Regular Grid.
  • Lithology block — an integer array shaped (nx, ny, nz) on a Regular Grid, where each voxel holds the formation ID of the youngest formation present at that location (0 = basement / no formation).
  • Octree cells (Octree Grid only) — the cells the grid ended up with, stored on the frame as cells (level and integer index of each cell). On an Octree Grid, the scalar fields, age masks, lithology block and fault domain map hold one value per cell, shaped (n_cells,) and in the order of cells.
  • Surface meshes — vertices and triangle faces per formation, stored under the mesh type keys masked, unmasked, combined, extended, extended_masked.
  • extended_masked is meant as input for 3D mesh generation of faulted models. Each fault domain contributes its own piece, extracted from the scalar field interpolated in that domain alone, so the pieces on both sides of a fault never have to be separated afterwards. The pieces are stored together in one mesh but share no vertices, so they can be split into connected components. Each piece is cut at the faults and at the base of all younger groups, and reaches about one grid cell beyond both, so it reliably intersects the fault and unconformity surfaces. Like extended, the pieces reach beyond the model boundary.
  • Fault surface meshes — masked, unmasked, extended and extended_masked meshes for each fault element. The fault's extended_masked mesh is cut at the base of all groups younger than the youngest group the fault offsets, and reaches about one grid cell beyond it.
  • All intermediate results — scalar values per element, age masks per group, and the fault domain map are stored on the structural frame within the result object and can be accessed programmatically for further analysis or visualisation.

The StructuralModelResults object is the direct input to the meshing components. The meshing components currently need a structural model computed on a Regular Grid and refuse a model computed on an Octree Grid (see the meshing manual).

docs.title: Save, load and export
docs.text:
Workbench components: Export Structural Model, Load Structural Model

A computed structural model can be saved as a file and loaded again, for example to compute a slow model once and reuse it in later workflows, or to pass it on to colleagues. Export Structural Model offers four formats:

Format Content Use wbgeo_sm The complete StructuralModelResults (one .wbgeo_sm file) Load it again with Load Structural Model gocad_ts One GOCAD TSurf file (.ts) per surface, in a ZIP Surfaces for modeling software that reads GOCAD (e.g. Leapfrog Geo, Petrel, SKUA-GOCAD) obj All surfaces in one Wavefront OBJ file with an MTL file for the colours, in a ZIP Surfaces for 3D viewers and modeling software (e.g. Leapfrog) vtk Each surface as VTK PolyData (.vtp), plus the lithology block, the scalar fields, the age masks and the fault domains as a VTK grid (lithology_block.vti on a Regular Grid, lithology_block.vtu on an Octree Grid), in a ZIP ParaView and other VTK tools

wbgeo_sm is lossless: the loaded model is the same StructuralModelResults that was saved, including the fault model, the input data and the interpolation methods and parameters, and can be connected to meshing, simulation and inspection like a computed one. The file is a ZIP archive with a manifest.json (format name and version, result type), a model.json (the result without its arrays) and an arrays.npz (all arrays, compressed). Files of older format versions stay readable.

The GOCAD TSurf, OBJ and VTK exports contain the masked surface of every formation (where the formation exists in the model) and the unmasked surface of every fault. These formats do not store the stratigraphic order, so each export also contains surfaces.csv, which lists the surfaces youngest to oldest with their group, kind (horizon or fault), colour and file. GOCAD TSurf files of faults are marked with GEOLOGICAL_TYPE fault. In the lithology block, the arrays are cell data on the model grid (on an Octree Grid, lithology_block.vtu has one hexahedron per octree cell): lithology, scalar_field_<group>, mask_<group>, fault_domain and scalar_field_<fault>.

In the Workbench, Load Structural Model takes a .wbgeo_sm file picked in the file browser.

In Python:

from core.structural_modeling_components.structural_model_file import save_structural_model, load_structural_model
from core.structural_modeling_components.structural_model_export import export_structural_model

save_structural_model(structural_model_result, "model2.wbgeo_sm")
structural_model_result = load_structural_model("model2.wbgeo_sm")

# surfaces for other software, as a ZIP
with open("model2_gocad_ts.zip", "wb") as f:
    f.write(export_structural_model(structural_model_result, "gocad_ts").getvalue())

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: Visualization is a core component of the Workbench, allowing for the inspection of geological models, simulation results, and input data in both 2D and 3D. The Workbench provides built-in plotting tools and a seamless integration with LiquidEarth for immersive visualization.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The Workbench uses a variety of visualization methods depending on the data type and the stage of the workflow:

  • 2D Slice Views: Cross-sections through volumetric data (scalar fields, lithology blocks, simulation variables).
  • 3D Interactive Plots: Powered by PyVista, these allow for interactive exploration of surface meshes, point data, and volumetric grids.
  • Detailed Reports: Text-based summaries of model results and input data.
  • Immersive Visualization (LiquidEarth): A cloud-based platform for visualizing and sharing 3D geological models in XR (Extended Reality), VR (Virtual Reality), and AR (Augmented Reality).

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Visualization is typically accessed via inspectors attached to Workbench components. When a component that produces a visualizable output is selected, the available visualization options appear in the inspector panel.

docs.title: 1. Visualizing Structural Models
docs.text:
Workbench components: Compute Structural Model, Compute Fault Model

Once a structural or fault model has been computed, it can be inspected using:

  • Plot Model Result 2D: Generates 2D cross-sections of the scalar fields and lithology.
  • Plot Model Result 3D: Opens an interactive 3D window showing the interpolated surfaces and/or the volumetric grid.
  • Detailed Report: Provides a summary of the stratigraphic groups, interpolation parameters, and data statistics.

These work the same for models on a Regular Grid and on an Octree Grid. In the codebase functions, the octree cells can be shown with show_grid (2D plots) and show_lith_block (3D plot); see the structural modeling manual.

docs.title: 2. Visualizing Simulation Results
docs.text:
Workbench component: Simulating with Sfepy

Simulation outputs (such as pressure, temperature, or displacement fields) can be visualized using:

  • Plot Variable p at a time: 3D visualization of a specific simulation variable at a selected time step.
  • Plot Variable T along a cross_section: 2D slice through the simulation domain.
  • Plot Variable p along a line: 1D profile of a variable between two points.

docs.title: 3. Visualizing Meshes
docs.text:
Workbench component: Plot Mesh in 3D

Unstructured and structured meshes used for simulations can be visualized in 3D, with elements colored by their lithology or property labels.

docs.title: LiquidEarth Integration
docs.text: LiquidEarth allows you to push your geological models to a cloud-based immersive environment.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
To use the LiquidEarth integration, you need an API token:

License Required Currently, a basic license is required to generate API tokens. Please contact info@terranigma-solutions.com so a license can be issued to you.

  1. Create an account at LiquidEarth.
  2. Generate an API token in your user profile settings.

docs.title: Pushing Data to LiquidEarth
docs.text:
Workbench component: Push Structural Model to LiquidEarth

  1. Connect the structural_model output of a Compute Structural Model component to the input of the Push Structural Model to LiquidEarth component.
  2. Provide your API Token.
  3. Specify a Space Name (where the model will be stored) and a Model Name.
  4. Run the component.

The component returns a Space Link.

docs.title: Opening in LiquidEarth
docs.text:
Workbench component: Open in LiquidEarth

The output of the LiquidEarth Workbench component will display a clickable link that opens the model directly in the LiquidEarth Application. If the Application is not installed it will link you to the installation page instead.

docs.title: Developer's Guide
docs.text: This chapter outlines the functionality of the internal, decorator-based DSL for component definitions and the infrastructure behind it.

docs.title: Abstract Description
docs.text: The structure of the workbench can abstractly be seen as a component and connector architecture. Developers will mainly interact with components (that compute something) and types (as in the input/output type definitions accepted by components).

docs.title: Architecture of the Visual Editor
docs.text:
At runtime the user interacts with the frontend/interface, which communicates with the orchestrator/backend.

The components itself are provided by runners which register the available type definitions and component definitions. The WBGeo-domain-specific MontiGem protocol is used for communication between the runners and the orchestrator. Internally, the MontiGem protocol is built upon WebSockets.

The interface, parts of the orchestrator, and the python domain classes are generated using the MontiGem framework from a set of input data and gui models.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
This section holds true for execution in the context of the visual editor. When running an example locally (e.g. as a .py file/jupyter notebook) the following steps do not occur (see below).

Each component is executed in a runner.

Before a component is executed:

  1. the runner loads the data of all inputs from a data storage
  2. then deserializes them to objects
  3. For WBGeo, pydantic is used to convert the data's JSON representation to python objects.
  4. Then the component is executed
  5. stdout, stderr, and errors are captures
  6. Finally, the result of the computation is serialized (using pydantic to JSON) and stored in the data storage.
  7. Additionally, a hash of the computation is stored among the hashes of all inputs.

docs.title: Simulated Data Flow in Python Notebooks
docs.text:
When writing example workflows, the (de)serialization step is omitted. To simulate it, you can add the following lines before importing any other files.

# Simulate the nodesapi at runtime to also check that (de)serialization is set up correctly
from examples.pydantic_nodesapi_simulation import register_as_test_nodes_api

register_as_test_nodes_api()
# ... rest of your program below

docs.title: Step 1: Git Clone
docs.text:
Checkout the codebase via git:

git clone git@github.com:wbgeo/codebase.git

docs.title: Step 2: Install Requirements
docs.text:
Install the requirements

pip install -r requirements.txt

On Windows, the sfepy package (used for process simulation) needs a C compiler to build during install. If you don't plan to run simulations and don't want to install a compiler, remove the sfepy line from requirements.txt before running the command above.

docs.title: Step 3: Done
docs.text:
And you are done. You can test out the examples to ensure your setup is working, e.g.:

python examples/synthetic_examples/model1/WBGeo1.0_model1.py

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A component is the building block of the workbench. They represent functions, turning inputs into outputs. (In the UI, they are represented by the rounded corner blocks. Square corners are used to show the results of a computation.)

@wbgeo_component(identifier='wbgeo::creation_create_random_number',
                 title='Create Random Number',
                 description='Create a random number', color='#03b1fc')
def create_random_number(start: int, end: int = 100) -> int:
   """
   Create a new random number within bounds
   :param start: int the lower bound
   :param end: int the upper bound (defaults to 100)
   :return: random number within the given bounds
   """
   return random.randint(start, end)

In this example, the function create_random_number is declared as a component. This is done via the @wbgeo_component decorator. Both of its parameters are declared as inputs. The second, end, parameter is optional (with a default value of 100). The function's signature MUST be explicit, i.e., contain a returned type and the type-hints of parameters.

The picture shows the visualization of this component.

Parameter Required Description identifier required A unique identifier. See below for a naming scheme title required The human-readable title shown to users of the workbench description (optional) The description shown to users of the workbench on request (if absent, the pydoc is used) input_checks (optional) The pre-checks (see below) color (optional) The color of the component border_color (optional) The border color of the component group (optional) The group this component belongs to positionInGroup (optional) The ranking of this item within the list of components of the same group tags (optional) For internal description return_name (optional) The name of the output port(s), default "result" is_object_type (optional) Some components should be presented like the result (e.g. the loading component), defaults to False requires_package (optional) The requirements which have to be installed for this component (e.g., wbgeo[sfepy])

The execution of the component MUST NOT modify/change its inputs, i.e. the inputs are immutable.

docs.title: Colours, groups and order
docs.text:
Colours are not chosen per component. They come from one palette in core/workbench_palette.py, so a workflow can be read at a glance. The colours follow the logo: brown and green for structural modeling, teal and blue for meshing, orange and red for process simulation. Within a step, substeps differ in lightness or a slight shift in hue, and exports take a shade of the step whose result they export:

Constant Colour Used for STRUCTURAL_INPUT #d4ad6e Input data and grid (Regular Grid, Octree Grid, Input data, Fault Input Data) FAULT_MODEL #9cc65a Compute Fault Model STRUCTURAL_MODEL #5fa040 Compute Structural Model STRUCTURAL_EXPORT #a9a845 Export Structural Model, Load Structural Model, Push Structural Model to LiquidEarth MESH #3a9fc4 Mesh creation MESH_ENGINEERING #7fd0cb Engineering objects (Load Wells, Sources, Shafts, Planes, Ellipses, ...) MESH_EXPORT #7896d0 Export Mesh SIMULATION_BUILDER #f9a93a Problem builders SIMULATION_RUN #e8663e Simulation runs SIMULATION_EXPORT #ec8468 Export Simulation Results PARAMETER #e6e6e6 Parameter types: file paths, tuples, selections, option forms BORDER #000000 Border of all components

The same rules apply to data types (see Types): a type that carries results between components takes the colour of the component that produces it (e.g. MeshResults uses MESH), and parameter types use PARAMETER.

The Workbench draws component text black in light mode and white in dark mode. Every colour has a contrast of at least 6:1 against black and about 2:1 or more against white; avoid very pale colours, white text is unreadable on them.

from core import workbench_palette as palette

@wbgeo_component(identifier='wbgeo::meshing_load_well_from_csv', title='Load Wells',
                 color=palette.MESH_ENGINEERING, border_color=palette.BORDER,
                 group='Meshing', positionInGroup=890)

When you add a component:

  • Reuse a colour first. A new component of an existing kind (another mesher, another problem builder) uses the existing constant. Add a constant only for a new kind of component (a new substep).
  • New substep: stay in the hue of the step (brown/green, teal/blue, orange/red) and stay clearly distinguishable from the sibling shades, also for colour-blind users.
  • New workflow step: take a new hue from the logo. The yellow between blue and orange (around #efb540) is still free.
  • Contrast: at least 4.5:1 against black (light mode) and about 2:1 against white (dark mode).
  • No literal colours in decorators; use the palette constants.

The sidebar lists the groups in a fixed order (Inputs, Meshing, Simulation, Visualisation, ...) and, within a group, the components by positionInGroup in descending order: higher numbers are listed first. Set both for every component, ordered as the components are used in the workflow:

  • each subgroup gets a block of 100, counting down: the first subgroup 990, 980, ..., the next 890, 880, ... (e.g. in Simulation: builders 990–950, runners 890–880);
  • inside a block, use steps of 10 so new components can be inserted;
  • exports always sit at 0, at the bottom of the group;
  • positions must be unique within a group.

tests/test_workbench_palette.py checks these rules (palette colours only, group and position set, unique positions, contrast). Colours, groups and positions are display only: changing them does not affect saved pipelines.

To be able to uniquely identify each component, you MUST follow the following naming scheme: identifier="wbgeo::[semantic_group]_[component_name]". For example, identifier="wbgeo::interpolation_rbf", tags=["Interpolation"]

The is_object_type parameter can be used to display the component like a result, which is just loaded. Like in the following example, the number 42 is loaded:

Similarly, when using non-controlled inputs, the input ports are always rendered:

docs.title: Multi-Outputs
docs.text:
By defining a fixed tuple as the output of a function, multiple outputs can be defined. Each item of the tuple is rendered as a separate output port. Each item's type must be a workbench compatible type, i.e. either a built-in, an annotated script type, or a wbgeo type.

@wbgeo_component(identifier='wbgeo::create_three_things',
                 title='Create Three Things')
def create_three_things() -> typing.Tuple[int, str, int]:
   """
   :return: returns three things
   """
   return 1, "example", 2

docs.title: User-Feedback
docs.text:
To provide feedback to a user, any output to the standard error stream results in the job completing with a warning.

import sys
print("This results in a warning, consider using a greater threshold value", file=sys.stderr)
Each warning should include hints to the user how to "fix" the possible problem.

Any thrown error results in the job failing with the exceptions message being used as the reason: 

raise ValueError("Data within the extent does not contain a good candidate for a magic unicorn. Consider using a different extend")
Each error should include hints to the user how to "fix" the problem. If possible, known constraints (e.g., a parameter must fall within a range, faults must not be present in the data, etc.) should also be checked via pre-checks (see below). (But pre-checks can be ignored, so they should be checked within the function as well).

docs.title: Pre-checks
docs.text:
Unlike errors during execution, pre-checks indicate incompatibilities before execution.

In case a component that has been executed (and thus, has a value present) is connected as an input to your component, all pre-checks are run. Pre-checks are functions referenced via the input_checks parameter of the components decorator. Their parameters must be a matching subset of the inputs of the function.

In case a pre-check raises an exception, users will be warned about the problematic connection.

def pre_check_my_interpolator(data: MyDataType):
    raise ValueError("Faults are not supported with the example interpolator. Consider using a different interpolator")

@wbgeo_component(input_checks=[pre_check_my_interpolator], ...)
def my_example_interpolator(data: MyDataType, treshold: int) -> MyResultType:
   # run the pre-checks first (at least those, that are really required)
   pre_check_my_interpolator(data)
   # do execution
   return MyResultType(...)

(Note: Only those pre-checks are run whose inputs have already been computed/are present. This requires the invocation of the checks during the execution again.)

docs.title: Inspection components
docs.text:
To enable users to inspect a result, special inspect functions can be defined. Their textual output (print(str)), matplotlib rendering, as well as pyvista plotter output is rendered on the UI. Unlike normal components, inspection components do not specify a return type. (By default, they also receive the __visualizer tag, hiding them from the default list of components.)

Note regarding the identifier: The semantic group of inspectors MUST BE inspect, followed by the identifier of the type, optionally followed by a suffix denoting the specific visualization used. Examples can be wbgeo::inspect_my_complex_data_type or wbgeo::inspect_my_complex_data_type_2d.

They can use an optional _inspector helper, which allows them to trace the computation's intermediate results.

@wbgeo_component(identifier='wbgeo::inspect_my_complex_data_type',
                 title='Visualize Example',
                 description='...')
@wbgeo_inspector()
async def _visualize_complex(i: MyComplexDataType, _inspector: InspectorHelper):
   #
   # Option 1: Use print(...) to output something
   print(i.name)
   print(":")
   print(str(i.numbers))
   print("----")

   # retrieve a value 
   # (note: this API is subject to change)
   trace = await _inspector.trace(MyListOfNumbers)
   if trace:
      print("value", await trace.get_value(), "end-value")
   else:
      print("no List of numbers found")

   # Option 2: Use the pv.Plotter
   import pyvista as pv
   mesh = pv.Cube()
   another_mesh = pv.Sphere()
   pl = pv.Plotter()
   pl.add_mesh(mesh, color='red', style='wireframe', line_width=4)
   pl.add_mesh(another_mesh, color='#03b1fc')
   pl.show()

   # Option 3: Use matplotlib
   import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
   import numpy as np

   xpoints = np.array([1, 8])
   ypoints = np.array([3, 10])

   plt.plot(xpoints, ypoints)
   plt.show()

docs.title: Import / Export components
docs.text:
While each computation's result is stored by the workbench, some workflows require interaction outside the workbench.

By using the nodesapi.BasicallyABufferedFile type as an input or as the resulting type, users can upload/import files to a workflow or download an export of data.

The following component exports data to a io.BytesIO buffer, when is then downloadable by a user:

from py_api_wbgeo.nodesapi import wbgeo_component, BasicallyABufferedFile
@wbgeo_component(title='Export MyListOfNumbers',
                 description='Export MyListOfNumbers to file',
                 group='Export',
                 identifier='py::export_MyListOfNumbers_to_file',
                 )
def export_to_file(mln: MyListOfNumbers) -> BasicallyABufferedFile:
  buf = io.BytesIO() # create new (buffered in memory) file
  # write to the buffer
  buf.write('My text...'.encode('utf-8'))
  # we can specify a name for the downloaded file
  buf.filename = 'numbers.csv'
  # as long as we return a BytesIO (buffered file)
  return buf

The component is visible on the left side of the following picture.

An example of an import is shown to the right and below: Here the import is

@wbgeo_component(description='Import MyListOfNumbers from F',
                 title='Import MyListOfNumbers from F',  # The title shown in the GUI
                 group='Import',
                 identifier='py::import_MyListOfNumbers',
                 return_name='mln'
                 )
def import_mesh_results_to_vtu(file: BasicallyABufferedFile) -> MyListOfNumbers:
  s = file.readlines()
  print("Loading file", file.filename)
  ret = [int(i.decode('utf-8')) for i in s[1:]]
  if len(ret) != int(s[0].decode('utf-8')):
    raise ValueError('Expected length did not match')
  return ret

docs.title: Dependant Inputs
docs.text:
One special kind of inputs are "dependant inputs", i.e. inputs that depend on another input.

For example: Given a list of group names and a CSV input file, the user should be able to select the group of each feature.

from py_api_wbgeo.smartcontrols import CtrlGroup, CtrlOrderedGrouping, SmartInputFormData, SmartInput

SmartStructuralInputSmartInputOptions = typing.Annotated[
  StructuralInputMappingOptions, SmartInput(inputs=['surface_points_file', 'group_names'],
                                          to_form=structural_input_smart_options,
                                          to_data=structural_input_smart_options_to_data)]


@wbgeo_component("...")
def structural_input_smart_options(surface_points_file: SurfaceCSVFileDataType,
                                   group_names: GroupNames
                                   ) -> CtrlGroup:
   return CtrlGroup(id='root', inner=[
      CtrlOrderedGrouping(id='groups',
                          label='Assign Groups',
                          groups=["c1", "c2"], # load this from the inputs
                          items=["a", "b", "c"], # load this from the inputs
                          )
   ]
                    )

@wbgeo_component(...)
def structural_input_smart_options_to_data(
      _input: SmartInputFormData,
      group_names: GroupNames,
) -> StructuralInputMappingOptions:
   input_as_json = smartcontrols.form_data_as_dict(_input)
   grouped = collections.defaultdict(list)
   if "root" in input_as_json and "groups" in input_as_json["root"]:
      for gn in group_names:
         if gn in input_as_json["root"]["groups"]:
            grouped[gn].extend(input_as_json["root"]["groups"][gn])

   return {k: tuple(v) for k, v in grouped.items()}


@wbgeo_component(...)
def my_component(
      surface_points_file: SurfaceCSVFileDataType = 'examples/synthetic_examples/model1/input_data/geological_data/model1_surface_points_df.csv',
      group_names: GroupNames = ['Strat_Series1'],
      mapping_object: SmartStructuralInputSmartInputOptions = {"Strat_Series1": ('rock2', 'rock1')}
) -> InputData_StructuralElements:
    pass

By using an annotated input type, with an annotation to SmartInput, an input type is defined as having "smart controls".

Parameters in the smart-input helper component functions with the same name and type as the real component will be passed along.

Please take a look at the smart controls file to see a list of available controls.

docs.title: Running the examples locally
docs.text:
You can either use Intellij with its python console to run the examples, or modify your PYTHONPATH environment variable:

# linux
cd codebase
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD:$PYTHONPATH"
python examples/synthetic_examples/model1/WBGeo1.0_model1.py

# powershell
cd codebase
$env:PYTHONPATH = "$PWD;" + $env:PYTHONPATH
python examples/synthetic_examples/model1/WBGeo1.0_model1.py

docs.title: Running the visual frontend locally
docs.text: See the visual editor installation guide for how to use a local codebase.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The workbench, by default, supports various built-in types. In the following table, the existing and supported python types are presented.

Python-Type Description bool A boolean value, represented as a checkbox in the UI int A numeric, integer value, represented as a number field in the UI float A floating point numeric value, represented as an number field allowing floating point values in the UI str A text value, represented as a text field in the UI List[?] A list of values, without an input representation in the UI Optional[?] An optional value, requires a default (e.g., Optional[str] = None)

docs.title: Annotating existing types
docs.text:
To help users by giving a type a semantic meaning, we can annotate types using AnnotatedScriptType, like in the following example:

from py_api_wbgeo.nodesapi import AnnotatedScriptType
MyListOfNumbers = typing.Annotated[
   typing.List[int], AnnotatedScriptType(name='numbers', color='aqua',
                                         identifier='MyListOfNumbers')]

The UI will handle them like their own type (due to the unique identifier), yet they are handled like their original type during the execution. For example, a special type for file paths could be added.

The identifier must be unique. (We recommend a namespaced identifier to avoid naming collisions.)

The AnnotatedScriptType accepts the following parameters:

parameter required description identifier required A unique identifier of this type name required The human-readable name of this type color (optional) The color of this type controlled (optional) If present, a value can be entered via the UI

Take the colour from core/workbench_palette.py (palette.PARAMETER for parameter types like the one above; see Colours, groups and order).

The UI additionally supports special input controls via the controlled parameter. By default, no special input controls are added.

Controlled= Description text A generic text input number A numeric text input password A generic text input with masked inputs boolean A boolean input RemoteFile|F1|...|Fn A selection of a file present in the codebase Select|O1|...|On A drop-down with the Options O1...On Table|C1|...|Cn A table with the columns C1...Cn and any number of rows List|C1 A list with the one C1 and any number of rows Tuple|C1|...|Cn A table with only one row (internal) See type BasicallyABufferedFile for uploading files (internal) See Dependant Inputs/SmartInputs; another layer of controls

To add support for additional input types, they have to be added to the UI (feel free to ask Alex for this).

docs.title: Defining more complex types
docs.text:
For types, that are not built-ins, you can define your own classes. We use pydantic (dataclasses or BaseModel) to define types.

from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass
from py_api_wbgeo.nodesapi import wbgeo_type

@wbgeo_type(name='Input data for a geological model', color='orange',
            identifier='wbgeo::my_complex_data_type')
@dataclass
class MyComplexDataType:
   name: str
   numbers: MyListOfNumbers

You must not use pydantics 'arbitrary_types' config option. Take a look at the pydantic_bridge adapters instead.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text: WBGeo can be used in two ways — choose the one that fits your use case:

docs.title: Visual Workflow Editor (Docker)
docs.text:
For: users who want to build and run geoscientific workflows through a browser-based visual interface, without writing Python code.

WBGeo runs inside a Docker container and is accessible at http://localhost:8080 once started. No Python environment setup is required.

Visual Editor Installation

docs.title: Python Codebase
docs.text:
For: users who want to work directly with WBGeo in Python scripts or notebooks — e.g., to run structural modeling, meshing, or simulation components programmatically.

Codebase Installation

docs.title: Codebase Installation
docs.text:
This document outlines an installation guide for using the workbench directly in Python scripts or notebooks.

See the visual editor installation instead if you want to run WBGeo through its browser-based interface in Docker.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
WBGeo requires Python 3.12.4 or later (earlier 3.12 releases fail to import the meshing components). We recommend installing into a virtual environment, e.g.:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate   # on Windows
source .venv/bin/activate   # on Linux/macOS

On Windows, the sfepy package (used for process simulation) needs a C compiler to build during install. If you don't plan to run simulations and don't want to install a compiler, clone the repository, remove the sfepy line from requirements.txt, and install from that local checkout instead of the git URL above:

git clone https://github.com/wbgeo/codebase.git
cd codebase
# remove the sfepy line from requirements.txt, then:
pip install .

docs.title: Install via pip
docs.text:
The core packages can be installed directly from source via:

pip install git+https://github.com/wbgeo/codebase.git

docs.title: Test Installation
docs.text:
You can test your installation by running one of the examples. Since the examples are not part of the pip-installed package, checkout just the examples/ folder via a sparse checkout:

git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/wbgeo/codebase.git
cd codebase
git sparse-checkout set examples
git checkout main

Then run one of the models, e.g.:

python examples/synthetic_examples/model1/WBGeo1.0_model1.py

docs.title: Visual Editor Installation
docs.text: This document outlines an installation guide for using the workbench with its visual editor. See the codebase installation for how to install the codebase to be use-able in Python scripts.

docs.title: Step 0: Install Docker
docs.text:
If you are unsure which variant of docker install, we recommend Docker Desktop to you.

  • On windows, you might have to toggle docker to use linux containers 1) right-click the Docker Desktop icon in your status bar 2) click the Switch to linux containers button

docs.title: Step 1: Download the docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
Download the docker-compose.yml file to your machine to a location of your choice.

This file tells docker how to orchestrate the containers required to run the workbench editor.

(In case you have already checked out the repository: You can use the docker-compose.yml directory in your git project instead)

docs.title: Step 2: Start the workbench editor
docs.text:
Switch to a CLI (e.g. cmd) and change into the directory of the downloaded file. (If you are unsure where your file is: Under windows: Shift-right-click the folder containing the file and select Open in Terminal.)

Run the docker compose up command in the CLI.

In case you receive an error during connect error: Ensure Docker (Desktop) is running.

docs.title: Step 3: Done
docs.text: Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. You might have to wait for the console to pause its output/the backend to be ready.

docs.title: How to use your own data with the graphical interface:
docs.text: By default, the docker setup mounts a own_data directory, which allows you to use your own input files. (Internally, they are mounted to examples/own_data.)

docs.title: How to update the graphical interface:
docs.text: Run docker compose pull, but Step 2 should update the images automatically. Certain updates might require you to also update the docker-compose.yml file, in which case you will have to perform Steps 1 and 2 again.

docs.title: How to reset the graphical interface:
docs.text: In case the application fails to start after an update, etc.: Run docker compose down to reset the interface. Then continue with Step 2 to start the interface again

docs.title: How to use a local codebase
docs.text:
In your docker-compose.yml file: Go to the services.py_runner.volumes key and uncomment/add the following lines:

services:
   py_runner:
      # ...
      volumes:
         - "./path/to/my/codebase/:/usr/src/app/codebase/"

Change the ./path/to/my/codebase/ path to point to codebase directory.

(Special case: If you are using the docker-compose.yml from the codebase's directory, uncomment the # option 1 lines instead.)

Now the container will start with your local codebase. After making changes to your local codebase, restart the py_runner container with docker compose restart py_runner to apply them.

In case you have modified the component signatures, you have to reset the stored components in the database: use the Reset page and then restart the py_runner container. The Runners page might help with dead runners.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
The docker image provides a set of configuration options. Some of these options are only available to the docker container, while others are set by default and are only available to the runner CLI script.

By default, the setup works without any modifications,

Environment Variable CLI Argument Description MINIO_HOST --s3 S3 Storage Host S3_ACCESS_KEY -s3-access Access Key (for S3) S3_SECRET_KEY --s3-secret Secret Key (for S3) BACKEND_HOST --backend Gem Backend Host PREPARE_TEMPLATES --templates Wheather to (default false) -p Python path of the runner -i Path to import for component loading LIQUIDEARTH_TOKEN Default token used for the LiquidEarth API.

@wbgeo_type(name="Fault Input Data",
            color=palette.STRUCTURAL_INPUT,
            identifier='InputData_FaultElements')
@dataclass
class InputData_FaultElements:
    """
    A class to represent the input input_data for a geological model.

        Attributes:
            name (str): The name of the model.
            fault_surface_points (pd.DataFrame): DataFrame containing surface points.
            fault_orientations (pd.DataFrame): DataFrame containing orientations.
    """
    name: str
    fault_surface_points: PandasDataFrame
    fault_orientations: PandasDataFrame  # Might be optional in future when not only UCK is used here
    fault_names: List[str]  # This allows us to use one input data file

    def __post_init__(self):
        # Remove duplicate fault surface points (same X, Y, Z, formation)
        _before = len(self.fault_surface_points)
        self.fault_surface_points = self.fault_surface_points.drop_duplicates(
            subset=['X', 'Y', 'Z', 'formation']).reset_index(drop=True)
        _removed = _before - len(self.fault_surface_points)
        if _removed > 0:
            print(f"[InputData_FaultElements '{self.name}'] "
                  f"Removed {_removed} duplicate fault surface point(s) (identical X, Y, Z, formation).")

        # Remove duplicate fault orientations (same X, Y, Z, formation)
        _before = len(self.fault_orientations)
        self.fault_orientations = self.fault_orientations.drop_duplicates(
            subset=['X', 'Y', 'Z', 'formation']).reset_index(drop=True)
        _removed = _before - len(self.fault_orientations)
        if _removed > 0:
            print(f"[InputData_FaultElements '{self.name}'] "
                  f"Removed {_removed} duplicate fault orientation(s) (identical X, Y, Z, formation).")
