def loss_grad(gradients_orie: torch.Tensor, y_true: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Orientation-gradient loss: cosine distance between the predicted gradient direction and
    the provided orientation vectors.

    Parameters
    ----------
    gradients_orie : torch.Tensor
        Predicted scalar field gradient at orientation point locations, shape (n_orien, 3).
    y_true : torch.Tensor
        True orientation vectors for the orientation points, shape (n_orien, 3).

    Returns
    -------
    torch.Tensor
        Mean (1 - cosine similarity) over orientation points.
    """
    grad_norm_pred = torch.norm(gradients_orie, p=2, dim=1)
    y_true_unit = nn.functional.normalize(y_true, p=2, dim=1)  # only the measured direction counts, not its length
    grad_inner_product = torch.einsum("ij, ij->i", y_true_unit, gradients_orie)
    cosine = grad_inner_product / grad_norm_pred  # normal orientation
    return torch.mean(1 - cosine)

docs.title: normalize(data, bounds)
docs.text:
Normalize coordinates into [-1, 1] using the provided model bounds, scaling all three axes by the same (largest) extent so the transform is isometric.

Using a single shared scale for x/y/z (rather than normalizing each axis independently to exactly [-1, 1]) preserves true distances/angles between axes. This matters here because the orientation loss (loss_grad) compares the network's gradient direction (computed in this normalized space) against real-world orientation vectors via cosine similarity - an anisotropic per-axis scaling would distort that comparison whenever the model's horizontal and vertical extents differ (the common case for geological models). This matches the default behavior of the reference GeoINR implementation (https://github.com/MichaelHillier/GeoINR), which uses the same isometric scaling for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: data : np.ndarray Array of shape (N, 3) containing xyz coordinates. bounds : tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float] Extent as (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax).

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
np.ndarray Normalized coordinates, dtype float32. The axis with the largest extent spans [-1, 1]; other axes are scaled by the same factor and so may span a narrower range.

def normalize(data: np.ndarray, bounds: Tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float]) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Normalize coordinates into [-1, 1] using the provided model bounds, scaling all three
    axes by the same (largest) extent so the transform is isometric.

    Using a single shared scale for x/y/z (rather than normalizing each axis independently
    to exactly [-1, 1]) preserves true distances/angles between axes. This matters here
    because the orientation loss (`loss_grad`) compares the network's gradient direction
    (computed in this normalized space) against real-world orientation vectors via cosine
    similarity - an anisotropic per-axis scaling would distort that comparison whenever the
    model's horizontal and vertical extents differ (the common case for geological models).
    This matches the default behavior of the reference GeoINR implementation
    (https://github.com/MichaelHillier/GeoINR), which uses the same isometric scaling for
    exactly this reason.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : np.ndarray
        Array of shape (N, 3) containing xyz coordinates.
    bounds : tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float]
        Extent as (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax).

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Normalized coordinates, dtype float32. The axis with the largest extent spans
        [-1, 1]; other axes are scaled by the same factor and so may span a narrower range.
    """
    # Centre and scale in float64 and only then convert to float32: real-world coordinates
    # (e.g. UTM northings ~5.8e6) are resolved to only ~0.5 m in float32.
    data = np.asarray(data, dtype=np.float64)[:, :3]
    centre = np.array([(bounds[0] + bounds[1]) / 2, (bounds[2] + bounds[3]) / 2, (bounds[4] + bounds[5]) / 2])
    range_max = max(bounds[1] - bounds[0], bounds[3] - bounds[2], bounds[5] - bounds[4])
    return ((data - centre) / range_max * 2).astype(np.float32)

def predict_stratigraphic_mlp(network: ConcatMLP, normalized_points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Evaluate a trained network at points already normalized with the training extent.

    Parameters
    ----------
    network : ConcatMLP
        Trained network (see :func:`train_stratigraphic_mlp`).
    normalized_points : np.ndarray
        Points of shape (N, 3), normalized with :func:`normalize`.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Flat predictions, shape (N,).
    """
    device = next(network.parameters()).device
    with torch.no_grad():
        points = torch.tensor(np.asarray(normalized_points), dtype=torch.float32).to(device)
        return network(points).cpu().numpy().ravel()

def stratigraphic_ConcatMLP(
    interface_data: np.ndarray,
    orientation_data: np.ndarray,
    meshgrid_data: np.ndarray,
    extent: Tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float],
    resolution: Tuple[int, int, int],
    in_dim: int,
    hidden_dim: int,
    out_dim: int,
    n_hidden_layers: int,
    activation: str = "Softplus",
    beta: float = 1,
    concat: bool = False,
    epochs: int = 2000,
    lr: float = 0.001,
    alpha: float = 0.1,
    lambda_g: float = 0.05,
    n_eikonal_samples: int = _N_EIKONAL_SAMPLES,
    seed: Optional[int] = None,
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Train a ConcatMLP to represent stratigraphic scalar field, then infer on meshgrid points.

    Parameters
    ----------
    interface_data
        Array with columns [label, x, y, z, ...]. Labels in [-1, 1].
    orientation_data
        Array with columns [x, y, z, dx, dy, dz, ...].
    meshgrid_data
        Array with columns [x, y, z, ...] for inference points.
    extent
        Model bounds as (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax).
    resolution
        Grid resolution as (nx, ny, nz).
    in_dim, hidden_dim, out_dim, n_hidden_layers, activation, beta, concat
        Network configuration.
    epochs
        Number of training epochs.
    lr
        Learning rate.
    alpha
        Weight for orientation loss.
    lambda_g
        Weight for the eikonal regularization term (`loss_eikonal`), sampled across the full
        domain each epoch. See module docstring for why this defaults to a nonzero value here
        (the reference implementation defaults it to 0.0).
    n_eikonal_samples
        Number of domain points (drawn once, from `meshgrid_data`, and reused every epoch -
        matching the reference's own static-sample approach) used for the eikonal term.
    seed
        Seed for the network's initial weights and the eikonal sample. With a seed, the same
        input gives the same result (on the same hardware); the global random state of NumPy
        and PyTorch is left untouched. None = different random start each call.

    Returns
    -------
    predictions : np.ndarray
        Flat predictions on `meshgrid_data` (raveled).
    iso_values : np.ndarray
        Unique interface labels (as used for isosurface extraction).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    normalized_meshgrid_data = normalize(meshgrid_data, extent)

    # static domain sample for the eikonal term (drawn once, reused every epoch - see
    # `loss_eikonal` and module docstring)
    n_eik = min(n_eikonal_samples, normalized_meshgrid_data.shape[0])
    eik_idx = rng.choice(normalized_meshgrid_data.shape[0], size=n_eik, replace=False)

    # Seeded runs use their own random state, so the caller's global NumPy/PyTorch state is
    # neither used nor changed.
    with _seeded_torch(seed):
        best_model, iso_values = train_stratigraphic_mlp(
            interface_data=interface_data,
            orientation_data=orientation_data,
            normalized_domain_samples=normalized_meshgrid_data[eik_idx],
            extent=extent,
            in_dim=in_dim,
            hidden_dim=hidden_dim,
            out_dim=out_dim,
            n_hidden_layers=n_hidden_layers,
            activation=activation,
            beta=beta,
            concat=concat,
            epochs=epochs,
            lr=lr,
            alpha=alpha,
            lambda_g=lambda_g,
        )

    # Predict with the model
    t1_inference = time.time()
    predictions = predict_stratigraphic_mlp(best_model, normalized_meshgrid_data)
    t2_inference = time.time()
    logger.info("Inference time: %.4f s", t2_inference - t1_inference)

    return predictions, iso_values

def train_stratigraphic_mlp(
    interface_data: np.ndarray,
    orientation_data: np.ndarray,
    normalized_domain_samples: np.ndarray,
    extent: Tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float],
    in_dim: int,
    hidden_dim: int,
    out_dim: int,
    n_hidden_layers: int,
    activation: str = "Softplus",
    beta: float = 1,
    concat: bool = False,
    epochs: int = 2000,
    lr: float = 0.001,
    alpha: float = 0.1,
    lambda_g: float = 0.05,
) -> Tuple[ConcatMLP, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Train a ConcatMLP on interface and orientation data (the training part of
    :func:`stratigraphic_ConcatMLP`). Seeding is up to the caller.

    Parameters
    ----------
    interface_data, orientation_data, extent, in_dim, hidden_dim, out_dim, n_hidden_layers,
    activation, beta, concat, epochs, lr, alpha, lambda_g
        As for :func:`stratigraphic_ConcatMLP`.
    normalized_domain_samples
        Domain points for the eikonal term, already normalized with ``extent``, shape (N, 3).

    Returns
    -------
    best_model : ConcatMLP
        The network with the weights of the epoch with the lowest loss, on the training device.
    iso_values : np.ndarray
        Unique interface labels (as used for isosurface extraction).
    """
    # read the input data
    train_data_x = interface_data[:, 1:].astype("float")
    train_data_y = interface_data[:, 0].astype("float")
    train_orie_x = orientation_data[:, 0:3].astype("float")
    train_orie_y = orientation_data[:, 3:6].astype("float")

    # normalize the input data
    normalized_train_data_x = normalize(train_data_x, extent)
    normalized_train_orie_x = normalize(train_orie_x, extent)

    device = torch.device("cuda:0" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

    normalized_domain_x = np.asarray(normalized_domain_samples, dtype=np.float64)

    # concatenate interface + orientation + eikonal-domain points into one training batch,
    # so a single autograd call (in the epoch loop below) covers all three
    train_x_dx = np.vstack((normalized_train_data_x, normalized_train_orie_x, normalized_domain_x))

    # convert to torch tensor and send to GPU
    x_dx_tensor = torch.tensor(train_x_dx, dtype=torch.float32).to(device).requires_grad_(True)
    y_tensor = torch.tensor(train_data_y, dtype=torch.float32).to(device)
    dy_tensor = torch.tensor(train_orie_y, dtype=torch.float32).to(device)

    # the number of interface/orientation/domain points, for dividing the stacked tensor
    n_intf = normalized_train_data_x.shape[0]
    n_orie = normalized_train_orie_x.shape[0]

    # train the model
    model = ConcatMLP(
        in_dim=in_dim,
        hidden_dim=hidden_dim,
        out_dim=out_dim,
        n_hidden_layers=n_hidden_layers,
        activation=activation,
        beta=beta,
        concat=concat,
    ).to(device)

    # amsgrad=True matches the reference implementation's optimizer (more stable updates via
    # a running max of past squared gradients). weight_decay is omitted - the reference's own
    # default for it is 0.0, so there is nothing to port there.
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, amsgrad=True)
    # Cosine LR decay over the full training run, matching the reference implementation.
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=epochs, eta_min=0)

    # Track minimum loss and corresponding parameters
    min_loss = float("inf")
    best_params = None

    t1_train = time.time()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        y_pred = model(x_dx_tensor)

        # single autograd call covers interface, orientation, and eikonal-domain points
        gradients = compute_gradients(x_dx_tensor, y_pred)

        # calculate the interface loss
        loss_i = loss_intf(y_pred[:n_intf, :].squeeze(), y_tensor)

        # calculate the orientation loss
        loss_o = loss_grad(gradients[n_intf:n_intf + n_orie, :], dy_tensor)

        # calculate the eikonal regularization loss (full-domain, not just at data points),
        # against a target gradient norm taken from what the network is actually achieving at
        # the real interface data this epoch (detached - it's an anchor, not something this
        # term should itself be allowed to optimize away from) - see `loss_eikonal` for why a
        # fixed target doesn't work for this module's label convention
        target_norm = torch.norm(gradients[:n_intf, :], p=2, dim=1).mean().detach()
        loss_eik = loss_eikonal(gradients[n_intf + n_orie:, :], target_norm)

        loss = loss_i + alpha * loss_o + lambda_g * loss_eik
        if loss < min_loss:
            min_loss = loss
            # copy: state_dict() returns the live weights, which the optimizer keeps changing
            best_params = {k: v.detach().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
            min_loss_i = loss_i
            min_loss_o = loss_o
            min_loss_eik = loss_eik

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward(retain_graph=True)
        optimizer.step()
        scheduler.step()

    t2_train = time.time()

    logger.info(
        "Training losses | Loss_i: %s, Loss_o: %s, Loss_eikonal: %s",
        min_loss_i.item(), min_loss_o.item(), min_loss_eik.item(),
    )
    logger.info("Mean epoch training time: %.4f s", (t2_train - t1_train) / epochs)

    # model for inference
    best_model = ConcatMLP(
        in_dim=in_dim,
        hidden_dim=hidden_dim,
        out_dim=out_dim,
        n_hidden_layers=n_hidden_layers,
        activation=activation,
        beta=beta,
        concat=concat,
    ).to(device)
    best_model.load_state_dict(best_params)

    # get the iso values for extracting the stratigraphic surfaces
    iso_values = np.unique(interface_data[:, 0])

    return best_model, iso_values

FDI solves the scalar field on its own regular cartesian support (finer with larger nelements) as a weighted least-squares problem: surface points (weight 1), orientations (orientation_weight) and smoothness (regularisation). class FDIParams(BaseModel):
    """
    Parameters for LoopStructural FDI (finite difference) interpolation.

    FDI solves the scalar field on its own regular cartesian support (finer with larger
    ``nelements``) as a weighted least-squares problem: surface points (weight 1),
    orientations (``orientation_weight``) and smoothness (``regularisation``). Only the
    ratios between the three weights matter. The solver is fixed to conjugate gradients
    with LoopStructural's default tolerance.

    Attributes
    ----------
    nelements:
        Number of elements of LoopStructural's support (larger = finer, slower).
    regularisation:
        Weight of the smoothness term. Default 0.1 instead of LoopStructural's 1.0: on
        synthetic model 2 it raised the agreement with the RBF model from 88.5 % to 95.6 %
        of the cells, whereas a finer support (more ``nelements``) gained at most about 2 %
        at many times the runtime.
    orientation_weight:
        Weight of the orientation constraints relative to the surface points.
    """

    nelements: int = Field(
        10_000,
        ge=1_000,
        description=(
            "Number of elements of the computation grid LoopStructural uses internally "
            "(larger = finer surfaces, slower)."
        ),
    )
    regularisation: float = Field(
        0.1,
        gt=0.0,
        description=(
            "Smoothness of the scalar field. Larger values give smoother, more planar surfaces "
            "that may not honour every data point; smaller values follow the data more closely."
        ),
    )
    orientation_weight: float = Field(
        1.0,
        gt=0.0,
        description=(
            "How strongly orientations count compared with surface points (1 = equally). Larger "
            "values make the layers follow the measured dips more closely; smaller values let the "
            "surfaces follow the surface points more closely."
        ),
    )

Parameters of GeoINR interpolation (implicit neural representation).

A small neural network (multilayer perceptron) is trained to output the scalar field at any location. Its loss combines three terms: the field value at the surface points (each formation has a fixed label between 1 and -1), the field's gradient direction at the orientations (weight orientation_weight), and a regularisation that keeps the gradient magnitude similar everywhere in the model (fixed weight).

Training starts from random network weights; seed fixes them, so the same input gives the same model.

Fixed (not exposed): Softplus activation with beta 1, no skip connections.

Older saved options may contain alpha (the previous name of orientation_weight, still accepted) and beta (now fixed, ignored).

class GeoINRParams(BaseModel):
    """
    Parameters of GeoINR interpolation (implicit neural representation).

    A small neural network (multilayer perceptron) is trained to output the scalar field
    at any location. Its loss combines three terms: the field value at the surface points
    (each formation has a fixed label between 1 and -1), the field's gradient direction
    at the orientations (weight ``orientation_weight``), and a regularisation that keeps
    the gradient magnitude similar everywhere in the model (fixed weight).

    Training starts from random network weights; ``seed`` fixes them, so the same input
    gives the same model.

    Fixed (not exposed): Softplus activation with beta 1, no skip connections.

    Older saved options may contain ``alpha`` (the previous name of
    ``orientation_weight``, still accepted) and ``beta`` (now fixed, ignored).
    """

    orientation_weight: float = Field(
        0.3,
        ge=0.0,
        validation_alias=AliasChoices("orientation_weight", "alpha"),
        description=(
            "How strongly orientations count compared with surface points. Larger values make "
            "the layers follow the measured dips more closely; smaller values let the surfaces "
            "follow the surface points more closely."
        ),
    )

    # --- network capacity / shape ---
    hidden_dim: int = Field(
        32,
        ge=4,
        description=(
            "Number of neurons per hidden layer of the network. More neurons can represent "
            "more complex geometry (e.g. tight folds) but train more slowly and may overfit "
            "sparse data."
        ),
    )

    n_hidden_layers: int = Field(
        2,
        ge=0,
        description=(
            "Number of hidden layers of the network. More layers can represent more complex "
            "geometry; 1 to 3 is usually enough."
        ),
    )

    # --- training ---
    epochs: int = Field(
        4000,
        ge=1,
        description=(
            "Number of training steps. More steps can fit the data better but take longer."
        ),
    )

    lr: float = Field(
        0.01,
        gt=0.0,
        description=(
            "Learning rate: step size of the training. If the result is unstable or "
            "differs strongly between seeds, try a smaller value (e.g. 0.003 or 0.001)."
        ),
    )

    seed: int = Field(
        0,
        ge=0,
        description=(
            "Start value of the random number generator. Training starts from random network "
            "weights; the same seed gives the same model. Try a few other seeds to see how "
            "much the result depends on chance."
        ),
    )

Bases: BaseModel

Parameters for LoopStructural PLI (piecewise linear) interpolation.

PLI solves the scalar field on a tetrahedral support (finer with larger nelements) with the same weighted least-squares terms as FDI.

In LoopStructural 1.8.2 the gradient constraint of the piecewise-linear interpolator is not implemented, so orientations are passed as tangent constraints (strike and dip vectors), weighted by orientation_weight. LoopStructural scales these with the element volume; the interpolator divides the weight by the mean element volume, so it does not depend on nelements.

class PLIParams(BaseModel):
    """
    Parameters for LoopStructural PLI (piecewise linear) interpolation.

    PLI solves the scalar field on a tetrahedral support (finer with larger ``nelements``)
    with the same weighted least-squares terms as FDI.

    In LoopStructural 1.8.2 the gradient constraint of the piecewise-linear interpolator
    is not implemented, so orientations are passed as tangent constraints (strike and dip
    vectors), weighted by ``orientation_weight``. LoopStructural scales these with the
    element volume; the interpolator divides the weight by the mean element volume, so
    it does not depend on ``nelements``.

    Attributes
    ----------
    nelements:
        Number of elements of LoopStructural's support (larger = finer, slower).
    regularisation:
        Weight of the smoothness term (constant-gradient regularisation;
        LoopStructural default for PLI: 0.1).
    orientation_weight:
        Weight of the orientation (tangent) constraints relative to the surface points.
    """

    nelements: int = Field(
        2_000,
        ge=1_000,
        description=(
            "Number of elements of the computation mesh LoopStructural uses internally "
            "(larger = finer surfaces, slower)."
        ),
    )
    regularisation: float = Field(
        0.1,
        gt=0.0,
        description=(
            "Smoothness of the scalar field. Larger values give smoother, more planar surfaces "
            "that may not honour every data point; smaller values follow the data more closely."
        ),
    )
    orientation_weight: float = Field(
        1.0,
        gt=0.0,
        description=(
            "How strongly orientations count compared with surface points (1 = equally). Larger "
            "values make the layers follow the measured dips more closely; smaller values let the "
            "surfaces follow the surface points more closely."
        ),
    )

def default_fdi_params(ctx: "InterpolationContext") -> FDIParams:
    """
    Derive heuristic default LoopStructural FDI parameters from an interpolation context.

    Heuristics
    ----------
    - `nelements` grows sublinearly with problem size: more data -> allow finer support,
      but keep a hard cap to avoid runaway compute/memory costs.

    Returns
    -------
    FDIParams
        A populated parameter object.
    """
    # Start from LoopStructural's common default nelements (~1e4) and scale with point count.
    # Use sqrt scaling so it increases, but gently:
    #   1k pts -> ~10k
    #   4k pts -> ~20k
    #   25k pts -> ~50k
    #
    # Clamp to keep memory/runtime predictable.
    base = 10_000
    scale = (max(ctx.n_points, 1) / 1_000) ** 0.5
    nelements = int(base * max(0.7, min(scale, 8.0)))  # factor in [0.7 .. 8.0]
    nelements = max(5_000, min(nelements, 200_000))

    return FDIParams(
        nelements=nelements,
    )

docs.text: Heuristic defaults for GeoINR based on problem size.

docs.title: Heuristic intent
docs.text:
• Two hidden layers; more neurons per layer for large datasets.
  • Large datasets: fewer epochs and a smaller learning rate, to keep the runtime bounded.

Calibration (synthetic model 2: all data and every third surface point; and the dipping-layer scenario of the integration tests, where the dip is known only from orientations; seeds 0-2 each): one hidden layer was worse than two in all three; 2000 epochs were worse than 4000 on the two sparse cases; an orientation weight of 0.3 was the best compromise (0.03 ignores the orientations in the dipping-layer scenario, 1.0 overweights the few orientations of the thinned model 2). Datasets with more than 500 points were not part of this calibration.

def default_geo_inr_params(ctx: InterpolationContext) -> GeoINRParams:
    """
    Heuristic defaults for GeoINR based on problem size.

    Heuristic intent
    ---------------
    - Two hidden layers; more neurons per layer for large datasets.
    - Large datasets: fewer epochs and a smaller learning rate, to keep the runtime bounded.

    Calibration (synthetic model 2: all data and every third surface point; and the
    dipping-layer scenario of the integration tests, where the dip is known only from
    orientations; seeds 0-2 each): one hidden layer was worse than two in all three;
    2000 epochs were worse than 4000 on the two sparse cases; an orientation weight of 0.3
    was the best compromise (0.03 ignores the orientations in the dipping-layer scenario,
    1.0 overweights the few orientations of the thinned model 2). Datasets with more than
    500 points were not part of this calibration.
    """

    n = ctx.n_points

    n_hidden_layers = 2
    hidden_dim = 32 if n < 3000 else 64

    # Epochs: 3000, 4000 and 6000 were equally reliable on model 2 (84/36-point groups,
    # one with a sharp local fold, 10 random seeds each), so 4000 for small datasets.
    if n < 800:
        epochs = 4000
        lr = 0.01
    elif n < 5000:
        epochs = 4000
        lr = 0.005
    else:
        epochs = 2500
        lr = 0.003

    orientation_weight = 0.3

    return GeoINRParams(
        orientation_weight=orientation_weight,
        hidden_dim=hidden_dim,
        n_hidden_layers=n_hidden_layers,
        epochs=epochs,
        lr=lr,
    )

def default_ok_params(ctx: InterpolationContext) -> OKParams:
    """
    Derive heuristic default Ordinary Kriging parameters from an interpolation context.

    Args:
        ctx: Context statistics (data scale, point count, NN distance).

    Returns:
        A populated :class:`OKParams`.
    """
    sx, sy, sz = ctx.data_scale
    npts = ctx.n_points
    nn_dist = ctx.mean_nn_distance

    # Range: use the data diagonal as the reference scale so that the range
    # covers the full data extent even when points are sparse at corners.
    # (Using only max(sx,sy,sz) would underestimate the range for data spread
    # across multiple axes, causing a "pillow" artefact with 4-corner data.)
    data_diagonal = float(np.sqrt(sx ** 2 + sy ** 2 + sz ** 2))
    range_ = np.clip(
        20 * nn_dist,
        0.1 * max(sx, sy, sz),
        1.5 * data_diagonal,
    )

    anisotropy_scaling_y, anisotropy_scaling_z = _kriging_anisotropy_defaults(ctx)

    # Neighbors (moving window)
    if npts < 20:
        neighbors = None  # global kriging
    else:
        neighbors = min(200, max(30, npts // 10))

    return OKParams(
        variogram_model=VariogramModel.GAUSSIAN,
        range=float(range_),
        nugget=0.0,
        anisotropy_scaling_y=anisotropy_scaling_y,
        anisotropy_scaling_z=anisotropy_scaling_z,
        neighbors=neighbors,
    )

• PLI's unstructured tetrahedral mesh is much more expensive per element than FDI's structured grid, so we start from a lower base nelements than FDI.
  • nelements grows sublinearly with problem size (sqrt scaling with point count), and is softly adjusted by how well-sampled the domain is (mean NN distance vs extent).

def default_pli_params(ctx: "InterpolationContext") -> PLIParams:
    """
    Derive heuristic default LoopStructural PLI parameters from an interpolation context.

    Heuristics
    ----------
    - PLI's unstructured tetrahedral mesh is much more expensive per element than FDI's
      structured grid, so we start from a lower base `nelements` than FDI.
    - `nelements` grows sublinearly with problem size (sqrt scaling with point count),
      and is softly adjusted by how well-sampled the domain is (mean NN distance vs extent).

    Returns
    -------
    PLIParams
        A populated parameter object.
    """
    # --- base scaling with problem size ---
    # PLI builds an unstructured tetrahedral mesh which is much more expensive per element
    # than FDI's structured Cartesian grid.  A lower base keeps runtimes reasonable for
    # small/medium inputs while still scaling up for large production datasets.
    base = 2_000

    # Sublinear growth with number of constraints.
    scale_n = (max(ctx.n_points, 1) / 1_000) ** 0.5  # gentle growth

    # --- sampling-density adjustment (optional but useful) ---
    # If points are dense relative to the domain extent, we can afford (and benefit from)
    # a bit more discretisation; if points are sparse, keep it conservative.
    extent = max(ctx.data_scale)
    if extent > 0:
        # dimensionless: bigger means denser sampling
        density = extent / max(ctx.mean_nn_distance, 1e-9)
        # Map density into a mild multiplier in ~[0.8 .. 1.4]
        # (log keeps it stable across huge ranges)
        import math

        scale_d = 0.8 + 0.1 * min(6.0, max(0.0, math.log10(max(density, 1.0))))
        scale_d = max(0.8, min(scale_d, 1.4))
    else:
        scale_d = 1.0

    nelements = int(base * max(0.8, min(scale_n, 10.0)) * scale_d)

    # Clamp: keep a low floor so tiny inputs don't over-allocate, and cap at 50k so
    # even very large models remain tractable without manual tuning.
    nelements = max(2_000, min(nelements, 50_000))

    return PLIParams(
        nelements=nelements,
    )

def default_rbf_params(ctx: InterpolationContext) -> RBFParams:
    """
    Derive heuristic default RBF parameters from an interpolation context.

    Args:
        ctx: Context statistics (data scale, point count, NN distance).

    Returns:
        A populated :class:`RBFParams`.
    """
    # Characteristic length scale (currently informational; may influence future defaults)
    cl = max(ctx.data_scale)

    # Always provide a shape parameter so that switching to a kernel that needs one
    # works without further input. SciPy scales distances by epsilon, so it is an
    # inverse length: a few nearest-neighbour distances per kernel width.
    nn_dist = ctx.mean_nn_distance if ctx.mean_nn_distance > 0 else max(cl, 1.0)
    epsilon = 1.0 / (5.0 * nn_dist)

    # Neighbors scale with problem size
    neighbors: Optional[int] = None
    if ctx.n_points > 5000:
        neighbors = min(500, int(5 * ctx.n_points ** (2 / 3)))

    return RBFParams(
        kernel=RBFKernel.THIN_PLATE_SPLINE,
        smoothing=0.05,  # categorical scalar field → smooth by default
        epsilon=epsilon,
        neighbors=neighbors,
        anisotropy_scaling_z=1.0,
    )

def default_uk_params(ctx: InterpolationContext) -> UKParams:
    """
    Derive heuristic default Universal Kriging parameters from an interpolation context.

    UK defaults are similar to OK, but the range is slightly longer (the field left
    after removing the linear trend tends to be smoother) and the anisotropy scaling
    is allowed above 1.
    """
    sx, sy, sz = ctx.data_scale
    nn_dist = ctx.mean_nn_distance

    # Range: a bit longer than OK
    max_scale = max(sx, sy, sz)
    range_ = np.clip(
        30 * nn_dist,  # OK used 20*nn_dist; UK often benefits from longer
        0.15 * max_scale,
        0.9 * max_scale,
    )

    # Anisotropy scaling (PyKrige 3D: x is implicit; scale y/z relative to x)
    sx_safe = max(float(sx), 1e-12)
    anisotropy_scaling_y = float(np.clip(sy / sx_safe, 0.05, 20.0))
    anisotropy_scaling_z = float(np.clip(sz / sx_safe, 0.05, 20.0))

    return UKParams(
        variogram_model=VariogramModel.GAUSSIAN,
        range=float(range_),
        nugget=0.0,
        anisotropy_scaling_y=anisotropy_scaling_y,
        anisotropy_scaling_z=anisotropy_scaling_z,
    )

def add_phantom_element(surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, float]:
    """
    Add a synthetic older element below a group that has only one element.

    The surface points are copied and shifted down by 10 % of their bounding-box
    diagonal (at least 1 unit), labelled ``PHANTOM_ELEMENT_NAME``. Interpolators
    that only use surface points (RBF, Ordinary and Universal Kriging) need at
    least two different values to fit a scalar field.

    Returns
    -------
    surface_points_with_phantom, shift
    """
    coords = surface_points_df[["X", "Y", "Z"]].to_numpy()
    bbox_diag = float(np.linalg.norm(coords.max(axis=0) - coords.min(axis=0)))
    shift = max(0.1 * bbox_diag, 1.0)
    phantom_df = surface_points_df.assign(Z=surface_points_df["Z"] - shift, formation=PHANTOM_ELEMENT_NAME)
    return pd.concat([surface_points_df, phantom_df], ignore_index=True), shift

def points_support_polynomial(points: FloatArray, degree: int) -> bool:
    """
    True if a polynomial trend of `degree` can be fitted through `points`.

    Needs at least ``POLYNOMIAL_TERMS_3D[degree]`` points, and for degree 1 the
    points must not all lie in one plane (for degree 2 not on one quadric surface).
    """
    if len(points) < POLYNOMIAL_TERMS_3D[degree]:
        return False
    if degree == 0:
        return True
    return int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(_polynomial_matrix(points, degree))) == POLYNOMIAL_TERMS_3D[degree]

def effective_neighbors(neighbors: Optional[int], n_points: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """Moving-window size for PyKrige: None (all points) if `neighbors` would cover all points anyway."""
    if neighbors is None or neighbors >= n_points:
        return None
    return int(neighbors)

def interpolate_group_ordinary_kriging(
    *,
    group: Any,  # expected: StructuralGroup-like (group.name, group.structural_elements, group.get_interpolation_params())
    grid: Any,  # expected: RegularGrid-like with grid.gridx/grid.gridy/grid.gridz 1D arrays
    group_surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
    group_orientations_points_df: Optional[pd.DataFrame] = None,  # unused here
) -> ScalarFieldAndValues:
    """
    Ordinary Kriging for a single structural group (pure function).

    Parameters
    ----------
    group
        StructuralGroup-like object. Expected members:
        - `name: str`
        - `structural_elements: Sequence[... with .name]`
        - `get_interpolation_params() -> OrdinaryKrigingParams-like`
          (variogram_model, range, nugget, anisotropy_scaling_y/z, neighbors)
    grid
        RegularGrid-like object providing:
        - `gridx`, `gridy`, `gridz`: 1D coordinate arrays (cell centers)
        - `resolution`: tuple[int, int, int] (not directly used by this interpolator)
    group_surface_points_df
        DataFrame of constraint points with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "formation"].
    group_orientations_points_df
        Optional orientations DataFrame. Accepted for API consistency but not used.

    Returns
    -------
    scalar_field : np.ndarray
        Interpolated scalar field evaluated on the grid.
        Shape matches pykrige's output for `execute("grid", ...)`.
    scalar_values_by_element : dict[str, float]
        Mapping element_name -> scalar value. Values are strictly increasing from
        oldest=1 to youngest=n (group.structural_elements is assumed youngest->oldest,
        so reversed order is used here).

    Notes
    -----
    - Assigns strictly increasing scalar values: oldest = 1, youngest = n.
    - Uses params from `group.get_interpolation_params()` (expected: OrdinaryKrigingParams).
    - Does NOT mutate `group`.
    """
    ok3d, scalar_values_by_element, n_points = _fit_ok(group, group_surface_points_df, group_orientations_points_df)
    params = group.get_interpolation_params()

    # Never ask for more neighbours than there are points in this fit (e.g. a fault
    # domain with few points): PyKrige then fills the neighbourhood with a dummy index,
    # and the kriging matrix becomes singular. Use all points instead.
    n_closest_points = effective_neighbors(params.neighbors, n_points)

    # PyKrige uses a slower looping backend when requesting a moving neighborhood.
    backend = "loop" if n_closest_points is not None else "vectorized"

    scalar_field, _ = ok3d.execute(
        "grid",
        grid.gridx,
        grid.gridy,
        grid.gridz,
        backend=backend,
        n_closest_points=n_closest_points,
    )

    return scalar_field, scalar_values_by_element

def ok_input_problem(points: FloatArray) -> Optional[str]:
    """
    Check whether Ordinary Kriging can be fitted to `points` ((N, 3), including phantom points).

    Returns a description of the problem for the user, or None if the points are sufficient.

    if len(points) < OK_MIN_POINTS:

            f"needs at least {OK_MIN_POINTS} surface points, but only {len(points)} "
            f"{'is' if len(points) == 1 else 'are'} available. Add surface points."

    return None

docs.title: Piecewise linear
docs.text:
LoopStructural PLI interpolation for a single structural group.

This module provides a pure interpolator function that: - assigns strictly increasing scalar values per element (oldest=1 .. youngest=n), - builds a LoopStructural GeologicalModel from surface points + orientations, - creates a PLI foliation (piecewise-linear interpolator), - evaluates the feature value on a RegularGrid, and a fit-only variant (fit_group_piecewise_linear) that returns the fitted feature for evaluation at arbitrary points (octree grids).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The function does NOT mutate the passed group.
  • group.structural_elements are assumed ordered youngest -> oldest (framework convention).
  • The scalar field is returned in ZYX shape (reshaped to the grid resolution, then transposed).
  • Orientations only constrain the direction of the layers at their location; they carry no scalar value, so they may lie anywhere, not only on an interface. In LoopStructural 1.8.2 the gradient constraint of the piecewise-linear interpolator is not implemented (P1Interpolator.add_gradient_constraints does nothing), so each orientation is passed as two tangent constraints instead (gradient perpendicular to its strike and dip vectors, weight tpw). This is what FDI's gradient constraint does internally. Tangents do not tell up from down; that comes from the formation values. With only one formation (all values equal), LoopStructural additionally turns the gradient rows into normal-vector constraints, which define which way is up.

docs.title: PLI-specific parameters
docs.text: All LoopStructural creation/evaluation parameters are sourced from group.get_interpolation_params().

docs.title: Expected attributes on params
docs.text:
• nelements: int | float Discretisation size passed to create_and_add_foliation. (For PLI this controls the piecewise-linear support/mesh density.)
  • regularisation: float Weight of the smoothness term, passed as regularisation.
  • orientation_weight: float Weight of the orientation (tangent) constraints, passed as tpw.

def interpolate_group_piecewise_linear(
    *,
    group: Any,  # StructuralGroup-like (name, structural_elements with .name, get_interpolation_params())
    grid: Any,  # RegularGrid-like (extent, resolution, grid_coordinates)
    group_surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
    group_orientations_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
) -> ScalarFieldAndValues:
    """
    LoopStructural PLI interpolation for a single structural group (pure function).

    Parameters
    ----------
    group
        StructuralGroup-like object. Expected members:
        - `name: str`
        - `structural_elements: Sequence[... with .name]`
        - `get_interpolation_params() -> params-like`
          The params object is expected to provide PLI-relevant attributes described in the module docstring.
    grid
        RegularGrid-like object. Expected members:
        - `extent: tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float]`
        - `resolution: tuple[int, int, int]`
        - `grid_coordinates: (N, 3) ndarray` (cell-center coordinates)
    group_surface_points_df
        DataFrame with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "formation"].
    group_orientations_points_df
        DataFrame with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "G_x", "G_y", "G_z", "formation"].

    Returns
    -------
    scalar_field : np.ndarray
        Evaluated scalar field on the grid in ZYX shape (shaped to `tuple(grid.resolution)`,
        then transposed).
    scalar_values_by_element : dict[str, float]
        Mapping element_name -> scalar value. Values are strictly increasing from
        oldest=1 to youngest=n (group.structural_elements is assumed youngest->oldest,
        so reversed order is used here).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If surface/orientation inputs are missing/empty or required columns are absent,
        or if the DataFrames include formations not present in the group.
    """
    model, scalar_values_by_element = _fit_pli_model(
        group, grid.extent, group_surface_points_df, group_orientations_points_df)

    # Evaluate on grid
    #
    # scale=True (not False): GeologicalModel.data's setter unconditionally
    # rescales input X/Y/Z into the model's internal frame (subtract origin,
    # divide by scale_factor) before the interpolator is built/solved -- so
    # evaluation must undo that same transform on the query points, via
    # GeologicalModel.scale(), or this samples the solved field at the wrong
    # locations whenever the grid's origin isn't (0,0,0) (or scale_factor
    # isn't 1). finite_difference.py already does this correctly.
    # Cell centers exactly on a face of the tetrahedral support mesh would
    # evaluate to NaN; evaluate_loopstructural_feature evaluates those again,
    # minimally shifted.
    regular_grid: FloatArray = grid.grid_coordinates  # (N, 3)
    sf_flat = evaluate_loopstructural_feature(model, group.name, regular_grid, scale=True)

    # grid coordinates are ordered with x slowest: reshape to (nx, ny, nz), transpose to ZYX
    scalar_field = np.asarray(sf_flat).reshape(tuple(grid.resolution)).T

    return scalar_field, scalar_values_by_element

class RBFFittedField:
    """
    A fitted RBF scalar field of one group, evaluable at any points (see ``FittedField``).

    Attributes:
        scalar_values: Element name -> isovalue, oldest = 1 .. youngest = n.
    """

    def __init__(self, interpolator: RBFInterpolator, scalar_values: Dict[str, float],
                 axis_scaling: Optional[FloatArray] = None) -> None:
        self._interpolator = interpolator
        self.scalar_values = scalar_values
        # vertical anisotropy: query points are stretched like the fitted points
        self._axis_scaling = np.ones(3) if axis_scaling is None else np.asarray(axis_scaling, dtype=np.float64)

    def evaluate(self, xyz: FloatArray) -> FloatArray:
        """Field values at points of shape ``(M, 3)``; returns shape ``(M,)``."""
        return self._interpolator(np.asarray(xyz, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1, 3) * self._axis_scaling)

    Parameters

        - `name: str`
        - `structural_elements: Sequence[... with .name]`

        grid_points: FloatArray = grid.grid_coordinates
    else:
        gx, gy, gz = np.meshgrid(grid.gridx, grid.gridy, grid.gridz, indexing="ij")
        grid_points = np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel(), gz.ravel()])

    scalar_flat: FloatArray = rbfi(grid_points * axis_scaling)
    scalar_field = scalar_flat.reshape(tuple(grid.resolution)).T  # (nx, ny, nz)

    return scalar_field, scalar_values_by_element

Kernels with a polynomial term (thin_plate_spline and cubic: a plane, quintic: a curved surface) need at least as many points as the polynomial has terms (4 or 10), and the points must not all lie in one plane (or, for quintic, on one simple curved surface). Otherwise SciPy fails with "At least N data points are required" or "Singular matrix".

def rbf_input_problem(points: FloatArray, kernel: str, neighbors: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[str]:
    """
    Check whether RBF interpolation with `kernel` can be fitted to `points`.

    Kernels with a polynomial term (``thin_plate_spline`` and ``cubic``: a plane,
    ``quintic``: a curved surface) need at least as many points as the polynomial
    has terms (4 or 10), and the points must not all lie in one plane (or, for
    ``quintic``, on one simple curved surface). Otherwise SciPy fails with
    "At least N data points are required" or "Singular matrix".

    Parameters
    ----------
    points
        (N, 3) coordinates that go into the fit, including phantom points.
    kernel
        RBF kernel name.
    neighbors
        Number of nearest neighbours used per evaluation point, or None for all.

    Returns
    -------
    A description of the problem for the user, or None if the points are sufficient.
    """
    degree = RBF_KERNEL_POLYNOMIAL_DEGREE.get(kernel, 0)
    n_terms = POLYNOMIAL_TERMS_3D[degree]
    alternatives = " or ".join(f"'{k}'" for k in _RBF_KERNELS_FOR_FEW_POINTS)
    n_points = len(points)

    if n_points < n_terms:
        return (
            f"the kernel '{kernel}' needs at least {n_terms} surface points, "
            f"but only {n_points} are available. Add surface points, or choose the kernel "
            f"{alternatives}, which also work with fewer points."
        )
    if neighbors is not None and min(neighbors, n_points) < n_terms:
        return (
            f"the kernel '{kernel}' needs at least {n_terms} neighbours, "
            f"but 'neighbors' is set to {neighbors}. Increase 'neighbors' or leave it empty."
        )
    if not points_support_polynomial(points, degree):
        shape = "in one plane" if degree == 1 else "on one plane or one simple curved surface"
        return (
            f"all {n_points} surface points lie {shape}, so the kernel '{kernel}' cannot be "
            f"fitted. Add surface points outside this plane, or choose the kernel {alternatives}."
        )
    return None

docs.title: Universal cokriging
docs.text:
Universal Co-Kriging (via GemPy) interpolation for a single structural group.

This module provides a pure interpolator function that: - builds GemPy SurfacePoints/Orientations tables from the given DataFrames, - computes a GemPy model for a single series (the group), - extracts the scalar field and per-surface scalar values, - rescales the scalar field so that element isosurfaces map to 1..n.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The function does NOT mutate the passed group.
  • group.structural_elements are assumed ordered youngest -> oldest (framework convention).
  • The scalar field is returned in ZYX shape (reshaped to the grid resolution, then transposed).

A fitted single-series GemPy model, evaluable anywhere through GemPy's custom grid.

GemPy keeps the solved kriging weights in its in-memory cache, so each evaluation only computes the kernel at the new points (about 50 µs per point on the CPU; GemPy's dense grid and its own meshes are switched off). Group fields are rescaled like :func:interpolate_group_universal_cokriging's, so the element surfaces sit at 1..n; fault fields stay raw, like the regular fault interpolation.

Element name -> isovalue (1..n when rescaled, else GemPy's own).

class GemPyFittedField:
    """
    A fitted single-series GemPy model, evaluable anywhere through GemPy's custom grid.

    GemPy keeps the solved kriging weights in its in-memory cache, so each
    evaluation only computes the kernel at the new points (about 50 µs per point
    on the CPU; GemPy's dense grid and its own meshes are switched off). Group
    fields are rescaled like :func:`interpolate_group_universal_cokriging`'s, so
    the element surfaces sit at 1..n; fault fields stay raw, like the regular
    fault interpolation.

    Attributes:
        scalar_values: Element name -> isovalue (1..n when rescaled, else GemPy's own).
    """

    def __init__(self, geo_model: Any, raw_scalar_values: Dict[str, float], rescale: bool = True) -> None:
        self._geo_model = geo_model
        self._raw_scalar_values = raw_scalar_values
        self._rescale = rescale
        if rescale:
            _, self.scalar_values = rescale_scalar_field_safe(np.zeros(0), raw_scalar_values)
        else:
            self.scalar_values = dict(raw_scalar_values)

    def evaluate(self, xyz: FloatArray) -> FloatArray:
        """Field values at points of shape ``(M, 3)``; returns shape ``(M,)``."""
        points = np.asarray(xyz, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1, 3)
        raw = _gempy_scalar_field_at(self._geo_model, points)
        if not self._rescale:
            return raw
        rescaled, _ = rescale_scalar_field_safe(raw, self._raw_scalar_values)
        return rescaled

docs.text: Affine rescaling of a scalar field so that element isosurfaces map exactly to 1..n WITHOUT clipping the field.

def affine_rescale_scalar_field(
    scalar_field: np.ndarray,
    scalar_values_by_element: Dict[str, float],
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, Dict[str, float]]:
    """
    Affine rescaling of a scalar field so that element isosurfaces map exactly to 1..n
    WITHOUT clipping the field.

    Parameters
    ----------
    scalar_field
        Scalar field array (any shape).
    scalar_values_by_element
        Mapping element_name -> scalar value extracted at the corresponding surface points.

    Returns
    -------
    scalar_field_rescaled
        Rescaled scalar field.
    scalar_values_rescaled
        Element scalar values after applying the same affine transform.
    """
    # Sort elements by scalar value
    items_sorted = sorted(
        scalar_values_by_element.items(),
        key=lambda x: x[1],
    )

    old_vals = np.array([v for _, v in items_sorted], dtype=float)
    n = len(old_vals)
    new_vals = np.arange(1, n + 1, dtype=float)

    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two elements for affine rescaling")

    # Use first and last element as anchors
    s1, s2 = old_vals[0], old_vals[-1]
    t1, t2 = new_vals[0], new_vals[-1]

    a = (t2 - t1) / (s2 - s1)
    b = t1 - a * s1

    # Apply globally
    scalar_field_rescaled = a * scalar_field + b

    # New scalar values per element
    scalar_values_rescaled: Dict[str, float] = {
        name: float(a * val + b)
        for name, val in scalar_values_by_element.items()
    }

    return scalar_field_rescaled, scalar_values_rescaled

def interpolate_group_universal_cokriging(
    *,
    group: Any,  # expected: StructuralGroup-like (group.name, group.structural_elements with .name)
    grid: Any,  # expected: RegularGrid-like (grid.extent, grid.resolution)
    group_surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
    group_orientations_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
) -> ScalarFieldAndValues:
    """
    Universal Co-Kriging (via GemPy) for a single structural group (pure function).

    Parameters
    ----------
    group
        StructuralGroup-like object. Expected members:
        - `name: str`
        - `structural_elements: Sequence[... with .name]`
    grid
        RegularGrid-like object. Expected members:
        - `extent: tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float]`
        - `resolution: tuple[int, int, int]`
    group_surface_points_df
        DataFrame with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "formation"].
    group_orientations_points_df
        DataFrame with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "G_x", "G_y", "G_z", "formation"].

    Returns
    -------
    scalar_field : np.ndarray
        Rescaled scalar field in ZYX shape.
    scalar_values_by_element : dict[str, float]
        Rescaled scalar values mapping `element_name -> isovalue` (targets 1..n).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If required input data is missing/empty, or expected columns are absent,
        or the DataFrames include formations not in the group.
    RuntimeError
        If GemPy returns an unexpected number of scalar values at surface points.
    """
    group_elem_names = [e.name for e in group.structural_elements]
    geo_model = _build_gempy_model(
        group.name, group_elem_names, grid.extent, grid.resolution,
        group_surface_points_df, group_orientations_points_df,
    )

    # ---- compute ----
    gp.compute_model(geo_model)

    # ---- fetch results ----
    scalar_values_by_element = _scalar_values_by_element(
        group.name, group_elem_names, geo_model.solutions.raw_arrays.scalar_field_at_surface_points[0]
    )

    raw_scalar_field = geo_model.solutions.raw_arrays.scalar_field_matrix[0]
    scalar_field = np.asarray(raw_scalar_field, dtype=float).reshape(tuple(grid.resolution)).T

    # ---- rescale scalar field so that element isosurfaces map exactly to 1..n ----
    # Piecewise affine (each interval between two surfaces separately). The global affine
    # alternative, `affine_rescale_scalar_field`, is not used.
    rescaled_scalar_field, rescaled_scalar_values_by_element = rescale_scalar_field_safe(
        scalar_field=scalar_field,
        scalar_values_by_element=scalar_values_by_element,
    )

    return rescaled_scalar_field, rescaled_scalar_values_by_element

docs.title: rescale_scalar_field_safe(scalar_field, scalar_values_by_element)
docs.text:
Rescale a scalar field so that element isosurfaces map to 1..n.

This uses a piecewise affine transform so that
  • for n == 1: a pure shift makes the only surface map to 1
  • for n >= 2: each interval between consecutive surfaces is rescaled independently

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: scalar_field Scalar field array (any shape). scalar_values_by_element Mapping element_name -> scalar value extracted at the corresponding surface points.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
S_new Rescaled scalar field. scalar_values_rescaled Target scalar values by element (exactly 1..n in sorted order).

Source code in core/structural_modeling_components/interpolator_functions/universal_cokriging.py 
def rescale_scalar_field_safe(
    scalar_field: np.ndarray,
    scalar_values_by_element: Dict[str, float],
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, Dict[str, float]]:
    """
    Rescale a scalar field so that element isosurfaces map to 1..n.

    This uses a piecewise affine transform so that:
      - for n == 1: a pure shift makes the only surface map to 1
      - for n >= 2: each interval between consecutive surfaces is rescaled independently

    Parameters
    ----------
    scalar_field
        Scalar field array (any shape).
    scalar_values_by_element
        Mapping element_name -> scalar value extracted at the corresponding surface points.

    Returns
    -------
    S_new
        Rescaled scalar field.
    scalar_values_rescaled
        Target scalar values by element (exactly 1..n in sorted order).
    """
    items = sorted(
        scalar_values_by_element.items(),
        key=lambda x: x[1],
    )

    old_vals = np.array([v for _, v in items], dtype=float)
    n = len(old_vals)

    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("No elements to rescale")

    # ------------------
    # n = 1 → pure shift
    # ------------------
    if n == 1:
        s0 = old_vals[0]
        shift = 1.0 - s0
        S_new = scalar_field + shift

        scalar_values_rescaled: Dict[str, float] = {
            items[0][0]: 1.0
        }

        return S_new, scalar_values_rescaled

    # ------------------
    # n >= 2 → piecewise affine
    # ------------------
    new_vals = np.arange(1, n + 1, dtype=float)

    slopes = np.diff(new_vals) / np.diff(old_vals)
    slope_lo = slopes[0]
    slope_hi = slopes[-1]

    S = scalar_field
    S_new = np.empty_like(S, dtype=float)

    # Below first surface
    mask = S <= old_vals[0]
    S_new[mask] = new_vals[0] + slope_lo * (S[mask] - old_vals[0])

    # Between surfaces
    for i in range(n - 1):
        lo, hi = old_vals[i], old_vals[i + 1]
        mask = (S > lo) & (S <= hi)
        S_new[mask] = new_vals[i] + slopes[i] * (S[mask] - lo)

    # Above last surface
    mask = S > old_vals[-1]
    S_new[mask] = new_vals[-1] + slope_hi * (S[mask] - old_vals[-1])

    scalar_values_rescaled: Dict[str, float] = {
        name: float(val)
        for name, val in zip([k for k, _ in items], new_vals)
    }

    return S_new, scalar_values_rescaled

def uck_input_problem(surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame, element_names: Sequence[str]) -> Optional[str]:
    """
    Check whether Universal Co-Kriging can be fitted to the surface points of one group
    (in one fault domain).

    GemPy takes the value of each formation from that formation's own surface points,
    so every formation of the group needs at least one point. (Orientations are
    checked separately.)

    Returns a description of the problem for the user, or None if the points are sufficient.
    """
    present = set(surface_points_df["formation"].astype(str))
    missing = [name for name in element_names if name not in present]
    if not missing:
        return None
    listed = ", ".join(f"'{name}'" for name in missing)
    return (
        f"needs surface points of every formation of the group, but there are none of {listed}. "
        f"Add surface points of {'this formation' if len(missing) == 1 else 'these formations'} here, "
        f"or use another method."
    )

docs.title: Universal kriging
docs.text:
Universal Kriging (3D) interpolation for a single structural group.

This mirrors the API and behavior of interpolate_group_ordinary_kriging but uses PyKrige's 3D Universal Kriging implementation.

Key behavior (same as the OK version): - assigns strictly increasing scalar values per element (oldest=1 .. youngest=n), - fits a 3D kriging model to surface points, - evaluates the scalar field on a regular grid, - does NOT mutate the passed group.

Universal Kriging additionally fits a linear trend (PyKrige's "regional_linear" drift, a + b·x + c·y + d·z) and always uses all points.

def interpolate_group_universal_kriging(
    *,
    group: Any,
    grid: Any,
    group_surface_points_df: pd.DataFrame,
    group_orientations_points_df: Optional[pd.DataFrame] = None,  # unused here
) -> ScalarFieldAndValues:
    """
    Universal Kriging for a single structural group (pure function).

    Parameters
    ----------
    group
        StructuralGroup-like object. Expected members:
        - `name: str`
        - `structural_elements: Sequence[... with .name]`
        - `get_interpolation_params() -> UKParams-like`
          Required attributes: variogram_model, range, nugget,
          anisotropy_scaling_y, anisotropy_scaling_z.
    grid
        RegularGrid-like object providing:
        - `gridx`, `gridy`, `gridz`: 1D coordinate arrays (cell centers)
    group_surface_points_df
        DataFrame of constraint points with columns ["X", "Y", "Z", "formation"].
    group_orientations_points_df
        Optional orientations DataFrame. Accepted for API consistency but not used.

    Returns
    -------
    scalar_field : np.ndarray
        Interpolated scalar field evaluated on the grid.
    scalar_values_by_element : dict[str, float]
        Mapping element_name -> scalar value. Values are strictly increasing from
        oldest=1 to youngest=n (group.structural_elements is assumed youngest->oldest,
        so reversed order is used here).
    """
    uk3d, scalar_values_by_element = _fit_uk(group, group_surface_points_df, group_orientations_points_df)

    # PyKrige's 3D Universal Kriging has no moving window: always all points.
    scalar_field, _ = uk3d.execute(
        "grid",
        grid.gridx,
        grid.gridy,
        grid.gridz,
        backend="vectorized",
    )

    return scalar_field, scalar_values_by_element

def uk_input_problem(points: FloatArray) -> Optional[str]:
    """
    Check whether Universal Kriging (with its linear drift) can be fitted to `points`
    ((N, 3), including phantom points). Otherwise PyKrige fails with "singular matrix".

    Returns a description of the problem for the user, or None if the points are sufficient.
    """
    n_min = POLYNOMIAL_TERMS_3D[_UK_DRIFT_DEGREE]
    if len(points) < n_min:
        return (
            f"fits a linear trend and needs at least {n_min} surface points, but only "
            f"{len(points)} are available. Add surface points, or use Ordinary Kriging, "
            f"which works with fewer points."
        )
    if not points_support_polynomial(points, _UK_DRIFT_DEGREE):
        return (
            f"all {len(points)} surface points lie in one plane, so the linear trend cannot be "
            f"fitted. Add surface points outside this plane, or use Ordinary Kriging."
        )
    return None

docs.title: Dual contouring
docs.text:
Dual contouring (DC) of fitted scalar fields on the max-level cells of an octree.

The octree counterpart of the marching cubes helpers in surface_mesh_extraction.py. Only cells at max_level take part: a surface reaches max level wherever refinement saw it, and :func:~core.structural_modeling_components.structural_modeling_utility.octree_refinement.balance_mesh_depth_adjacency makes sure the cells around it are at max level as well.

For one isovalue:

1) Field values at the corners of the cells, each lattice point evaluated once per cell group (cells of different groups, e.g. fault domains, never share corner values or faces). 2) One crossing per distinct cell edge whose end values lie on opposite sides of the isovalue, placed by linear interpolation along the edge, with the field gradient there as its normal (central differences of the field). Which side a value equal to the isovalue is on must match the labels the octree was refined with (>= for horizons, like the lithology; > for faults, like their masks); otherwise a crossing at a lattice point can fall into cells that were never refined. 3) One vertex per cell with a crossing, from GemPy's QEF: a row per crossing (its normal through its point) plus three axis-aligned rows through the crossings' centroid, all at unit weight; the vertex is clamped to the cell. 4) One quad per crossing edge from the 4 cells around it, split into two triangles whose normals point toward increasing field values. An edge with fewer than 4 such cells gets no quad: at the extent walls and next to cells of another group the surface ends there, next to a coarser cell this is a gap. With a cell mask (MASKED meshes), a quad is kept only if all 4 of its cells are kept.

EXTENDED meshes run on the cells plus a padding shell outside the extent (:func:padding_shell), on a lattice padded by the same number of cells.

Ported from the flat dual-contouring path of the octree research code (itself a port of GemPy's), adapted to explicit isovalues, integer cell addresses and cell groups.

def contour_cells(grid: OctreeGrid, cells: OctreeCells) -> OctreeCells:
    """
    The max-level cells dual contouring runs on, after the grid's gap mitigation.

    Args:
        grid: The octree grid; its ``gap_mitigation`` decides whether the cells are
            balanced first (:func:`balance_mesh_depth_adjacency`).
        cells: Leaf cells that tile the extent, refined toward the surfaces.

    Returns:
        Only the max-level cells, from a balanced copy if mitigation is on.
        ``cells`` itself is not changed.
    """
    if grid.gap_mitigation == GapMitigation.BALANCE_MESH_DEPTH_ADJACENCY:
        cells = balance_mesh_depth_adjacency(grid, cells)
    fine = cells.level == grid.max_level
    return OctreeCells(level=cells.level[fine], ijk=cells.ijk[fine])

def dual_contour(
        grid: OctreeGrid,
        cell_ijk: npt.NDArray[np.integer],
        cell_groups: npt.NDArray[np.integer],
        values: GroupFieldValues,
        isovalues: Sequence[float],
        strictly_above: bool = False,
        cell_kept: Optional[npt.NDArray[np.bool_]] = None,
        padding: int = 0,
        field_bounds: Optional[Tuple[float, float, float, float, float, float]] = None,
) -> List[DualContourMesh]:
    """
    Dual-contour one field at several isovalues on max-level cells.

    Args:
        grid: The octree grid.
        cell_ijk: Max-level cell indices, shape ``(M, 3)``, without duplicates.
        cell_groups: Group of each cell, shape ``(M,)``. Corner values are
            evaluated per group and quads only join cells of one group.
        values: The field; see :data:`GroupFieldValues`.
        isovalues: The isovalues to extract.
        strictly_above: Count a value as above the isovalue only if it is
            greater (``>``) instead of greater or equal (``>=``). Must match the
            labels the cells were refined with.
        cell_kept: Optional mask of the cells, shape ``(M,)``. A quad is kept
            only if all 4 of its cells are kept; vertices no kept quad uses are
            dropped. Quads dropped this way are no gaps. ``None`` keeps all.
        padding: Cells may lie up to this many finest cells outside the extent
            (see :func:`padding_shell`); the walls are those of the padded box.
        field_bounds: Optional ``(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax)`` the field
            is defined in; the points of the normals' difference stencils are
            clamped into it.

    Returns:
        One :class:`DualContourMesh` per isovalue.
    """
    ijk = np.asarray(cell_ijk, dtype=np.int64).reshape(-1, 3)
    groups = np.asarray(cell_groups, dtype=np.int64).reshape(-1)
    kept = np.ones(ijk.shape[0], dtype=bool) if cell_kept is None else np.asarray(cell_kept, dtype=bool).reshape(-1)
    if ijk.shape[0] == 0:
        return [_empty_mesh() for _ in isovalues]

    spacing = np.asarray(grid.finest_spacing, dtype=np.float64)
    # The lattice: [-padding, finest_resolution + padding) along each axis.
    n_finest = np.array(grid.finest_resolution, dtype=np.int64)
    n_lattice = n_finest + 2 * padding

    # Keys, one int64 each, ordered like the rows (x, y, z, [axis,] group): lattice
    # points (corners) are numbered over the padded lattice, groups by rank.
    group_ids, group_rank = np.unique(groups, return_inverse=True)
    n_groups = group_ids.size
    group_rank = group_rank.reshape(-1).astype(np.int64)
    n_points = n_lattice + 1                                                     # lattice points per axis
    shifted = ijk + padding
    cell_point = (shifted[:, 0] * n_points[1] + shifted[:, 1]) * n_points[2] + shifted[:, 2]  # lower corner
    corner_step = (CORNER_OFFSETS[:, 0] * n_points[1] + CORNER_OFFSETS[:, 1]) * n_points[2] + CORNER_OFFSETS[:, 2]

    # Corner values, each (lattice point, group) once.
    corner_keys = (cell_point[:, None] + corner_step[None, :]) * n_groups + group_rank[:, None]  # (M, 8)
    corner_unique, corner_inverse = _unique_keys(corner_keys.reshape(-1), int(np.prod(n_points)) * n_groups)
    del corner_keys
    corner_points, corner_group = np.divmod(corner_unique, n_groups)
    corner_values = np.asarray(
        values(grid.origin + (_lattice_coordinates(corner_points, n_points) - padding) * spacing,
               group_ids[corner_group]), dtype=np.float64)
    corner_values = corner_values[corner_inverse].reshape(-1, 8)                # (M, 8)
    del corner_unique, corner_inverse, corner_points, corner_group

    # From here on only the cells with a crossing: the 4 cells of a quad all contain
    # its crossing edge, so cells whose corners lie on one side of every isovalue
    # (e.g. cells refined for another group's surfaces) give neither vertices nor
    # quads. The look-up of neighbours below still sees all cells.
    all_ijk, all_groups = ijk, groups
    crossed = np.zeros(ijk.shape[0], dtype=bool)
    for isovalue in isovalues:
        above = corner_values > isovalue if strictly_above else corner_values >= isovalue
        crossed |= above.any(axis=1) & ~above.all(axis=1)
    cell_rows = np.flatnonzero(crossed)
    if cell_rows.size == 0:
        return [_empty_mesh() for _ in isovalues]
    ijk, groups, kept = ijk[cell_rows], groups[cell_rows], kept[cell_rows]
    cell_point, group_rank, corner_values = cell_point[cell_rows], group_rank[cell_rows], corner_values[cell_rows]
    del crossed

    # Edges: key = (lower-end lattice point, axis, group); each cell has 12.
    edge_keys = ((cell_point[:, None] + corner_step[_EDGES[:, 0]][None, :]) * 3
                 + _EDGE_AXIS[None, :]) * n_groups + group_rank[:, None]         # (M, 12)
    edge_unique, edge_inverse = _unique_keys(edge_keys.reshape(-1), int(np.prod(n_points)) * 3 * n_groups)
    del edge_keys
    edge_inverse = edge_inverse.reshape(-1, 12)                                  # (M, 12)
    n_edges = edge_unique.size
    edge_rest, edge_group_rank = np.divmod(edge_unique, n_groups)
    edge_points, axis = np.divmod(edge_rest, 3)
    lo_pt = _lattice_coordinates(edge_points, n_points) - padding                # (E, 3)
    edge_group = group_ids[edge_group_rank]
    del edge_unique, edge_rest, edge_points, edge_group_rank
    first = np.empty(n_edges, dtype=np.int64)
    first[edge_inverse.reshape(-1)] = np.arange(edge_inverse.size, dtype=np.int64)  # any incidence of each edge
    first_cell, first_edge = np.divmod(first, 12)
    va = corner_values[first_cell, _EDGES[first_edge, 0]]
    vb = corner_values[first_cell, _EDGES[first_edge, 1]]
    del first, first_cell, first_edge

    # The 4 cells around each edge, in cyclic order. A cell sees an edge at its
    # corner offsets (o1, o2) along the two other axes, taken in right-handed
    # order (y, z), (z, x), (x, y); the slot follows from them.
    other_axes = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 0], [0, 1]], dtype=np.int64)
    offsets = CORNER_OFFSETS[_EDGES[:, 0]]                                       # (12, 3)
    o = offsets[np.arange(12)[:, None], other_axes[_EDGE_AXIS]]                  # (12, 2)
    slot_of = np.array([[0, 3], [1, 2]], dtype=np.int64)                         # (o1, o2) -> slot
    edge_slot = slot_of[o[:, 0], o[:, 1]]                                        # (12,)
    ring = np.full((n_edges, 4), -1, dtype=np.int32)
    ring[edge_inverse, edge_slot[None, :]] = np.arange(ijk.shape[0], dtype=np.int32)[:, None]

    # An edge on the extent's outer faces can't have 4 cells around it.
    on_wall = np.zeros(n_edges, dtype=bool)
    for a in range(3):
        across = axis != a
        on_wall |= across & ((lo_pt[:, a] == -padding) | (lo_pt[:, a] == n_finest[a] + padding))

    # Look-up of all cells by position (rows of all_ijk), to tell another group's cell
    # from no cell: a dense array of cell rows over the lattice where it fits, else a
    # sorted search.
    keys = linear_cell_index(all_ijk + padding, n_lattice)
    if int(np.prod(n_lattice)) <= _DENSE_LOOKUP_MAX_ENTRIES:
        row_at = np.full(int(np.prod(n_lattice)), -1, dtype=np.int32)
        row_at[keys] = np.arange(all_ijk.shape[0], dtype=np.int32)

        def rows_at(k: IntArray) -> IntArray:
            return row_at[k]
    else:
        order = np.argsort(keys)
        sorted_keys = keys[order]

        def rows_at(k: IntArray) -> IntArray:
            pos = np.minimum(np.searchsorted(sorted_keys, k), sorted_keys.size - 1)
            return np.where(sorted_keys[pos] == k, order[pos], -1)

    def find(points_ijk: IntArray) -> IntArray:
        """Row (in all_ijk) of the cell at each position, -1 where there is none."""
        shifted = points_ijk + padding
        inside = np.all((shifted >= 0) & (shifted < n_lattice), axis=1)
        k = linear_cell_index(np.where(inside[:, None], shifted, 0), n_lattice)
        return np.where(inside, rows_at(k), -1)

    at_group_boundary = np.zeros(ijk.shape[0], dtype=bool)
    for step in _NEIGHBOUR_STEPS:
        neighbour = find(ijk + step)
        at_group_boundary |= (neighbour >= 0) & (all_groups[np.maximum(neighbour, 0)] != groups)
    slot_offsets = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1], [0, 1]], dtype=np.int64)  # (o1, o2) per slot

    h = _GRADIENT_STEP_CELLS * spacing
    if field_bounds is None:
        bounds_lo, bounds_hi = np.full(3, -np.inf), np.full(3, np.inf)
    else:
        bounds_lo, bounds_hi = np.array(field_bounds[0::2]), np.array(field_bounds[1::2])
    cell_min = grid.origin + ijk * spacing
    meshes = []
    for isovalue in isovalues:
        if strictly_above:
            crossing = (va > isovalue) != (vb > isovalue)
        else:
            crossing = (va >= isovalue) != (vb >= isovalue)
        idx = np.flatnonzero(crossing)
        if idx.size == 0:
            meshes.append(_empty_mesh())
            continue

        # Crossing points and normals.
        t = (isovalue - va[idx]) / (vb[idx] - va[idx])
        direction = np.eye(3)[axis[idx]]
        points = grid.origin + (lo_pt[idx] + t[:, None] * direction) * spacing
        edge_groups = edge_group[idx]
        # All 6 stencil points in one call: every call into GemPy recompiles its
        # backend, which leaks Windows DLL-directory handles over many calls.
        steps = np.concatenate([np.diag(h), -np.diag(h)])                        # +x, +y, +z, -x, -y, -z
        stencil = np.clip(points[None, :, :] + steps[:, None, :], bounds_lo, bounds_hi)
        stencil_values = np.asarray(
            values(stencil.reshape(-1, 3), np.tile(edge_groups, 6)), dtype=np.float64).reshape(6, -1)
        distance = stencil[:3, :, :] - stencil[3:, :, :]                          # (3, K, 3)
        normals = ((stencil_values[:3] - stencil_values[3:])
                   / distance[np.arange(3), :, np.arange(3)]).T
        norm = np.linalg.norm(normals, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        normals = normals / np.where(norm > 1e-12, norm, 1.0)

        # QEF per cell over its crossing edges.
        crossing_number = np.full(n_edges, -1, dtype=np.int32)
        crossing_number[idx] = np.arange(idx.size, dtype=np.int32)
        cell_cross = crossing_number[edge_inverse]                               # (M, 12)
        valid = cell_cross >= 0
        has_vertex = valid.any(axis=1)
        cv = cell_cross[has_vertex]
        valid_v = valid[has_vertex]
        p = np.where(valid_v[..., None], points[np.maximum(cv, 0)], 0.0)        # (V, 12, 3)
        n = np.where(valid_v[..., None], normals[np.maximum(cv, 0)], 0.0)
        mass = p.sum(axis=1) / valid_v.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        a_rows = np.concatenate([n, np.broadcast_to(np.eye(3), (cv.shape[0], 3, 3))], axis=1)
        b_rows = np.concatenate([np.einsum("vri,vri->vr", n, p), mass], axis=1)
        ata = np.einsum("vri,vrj->vij", a_rows, a_rows)
        atb = np.einsum("vri,vr->vi", a_rows, b_rows)
        vertices = np.linalg.solve(ata, atb[..., None])[..., 0]
        lo = cell_min[has_vertex]
        vertices = np.clip(vertices, lo, lo + spacing)

        # Quads around crossing edges with all 4 cells present.
        vertex_of_cell = np.full(ijk.shape[0], -1, dtype=np.int64)
        vertex_of_cell[has_vertex] = np.arange(int(has_vertex.sum()))
        quads = ring[idx]
        complete = np.all(quads >= 0, axis=1)
        gap = np.zeros(quads.shape[0], dtype=bool)
        for slot in range(4):
            empty = np.flatnonzero((quads[:, slot] < 0) & ~on_wall[idx])
            if empty.size == 0:
                continue
            # The cell that would fill the slot: is it another group's or absent?
            e = idx[empty]
            cell = lo_pt[e].copy()
            axes = other_axes[axis[e]]
            rows = np.arange(e.size)
            cell[rows, axes[:, 0]] -= slot_offsets[slot, 0]
            cell[rows, axes[:, 1]] -= slot_offsets[slot, 1]
            gap[empty[find(cell) < 0]] = True
        # Only gaps among kept cells count; quads with a masked cell are dropped anyway.
        all_kept = np.all(np.where(quads >= 0, kept[np.maximum(quads, 0)], True), axis=1)
        n_missing = int(np.sum(gap & all_kept))
        complete &= all_kept
        quads = vertex_of_cell[quads[complete]]
        # Slots run counter-clockwise around the edge's axis seen from its +
        # end, so the quad normal points along +axis; flip where the field
        # decreases along the edge.
        increasing = (vb[idx] > va[idx])[complete]
        quads = np.where(increasing[:, None], quads, quads[:, ::-1])
        faces = np.concatenate([quads[:, [0, 1, 2]], quads[:, [0, 2, 3]]], axis=0)
        vertex_rows = cell_rows[has_vertex]                                     # rows of cell_ijk
        boundary = at_group_boundary[has_vertex]
        if cell_kept is not None:
            vertices, faces, used = select_faces(vertices, faces, np.ones(faces.shape[0], dtype=bool))
            vertex_rows, boundary = vertex_rows[used], boundary[used]
        meshes.append(DualContourMesh(
            vertices=vertices, faces=faces.astype(np.int64), vertex_cells=all_ijk[vertex_rows],
            vertex_rows=vertex_rows, vertex_at_group_boundary=boundary, n_missing_quads=n_missing,
        ))
    return meshes

docs.title: interior_open_edges(mesh, grid, padding=0)
docs.text:
Number of open mesh edges (used by one triangle) that border a gap.

A surface legitimately ends half a cell inside a wall of the extent and half a cell before a cell of another group: an open edge whose two vertices both come from cells next to the same wall, or both from cells next to another group, is such an end. Every other open edge borders a gap in the surface. With padding (EXTENDED meshes), the walls are those of the padded box.

Source code in core/structural_modeling_components/structural_modeling_utility/dual_contouring.py 
def interior_open_edges(mesh: DualContourMesh, grid: OctreeGrid, padding: int = 0) -> int:
    """
    Number of open mesh edges (used by one triangle) that border a gap.

    A surface legitimately ends half a cell inside a wall of the extent and half a
    cell before a cell of another group: an open edge whose two vertices both come
    from cells next to the same wall, or both from cells next to another group, is
    such an end. Every other open edge borders a gap in the surface. With
    ``padding`` (EXTENDED meshes), the walls are those of the padded box.
    """
    if mesh.faces.shape[0] == 0:
        return 0
    edges = np.sort(np.concatenate([mesh.faces[:, [0, 1]], mesh.faces[:, [1, 2]], mesh.faces[:, [2, 0]]]), axis=1)
    unique, counts = np.unique(edges, axis=0, return_counts=True)
    open_edges = unique[counts == 1]
    n_finest = np.array(grid.finest_resolution, dtype=np.int64)
    near_wall = np.concatenate([mesh.vertex_cells == -padding, mesh.vertex_cells == n_finest - 1 + padding],
                               axis=1)  # (V, 6)
    on_wall = np.any(near_wall[open_edges[:, 0]] & near_wall[open_edges[:, 1]], axis=1)
    at_boundary = mesh.vertex_at_group_boundary[open_edges[:, 0]] & mesh.vertex_at_group_boundary[open_edges[:, 1]]
    return int(np.sum(~on_wall & ~at_boundary))

def padding_shell(grid: OctreeGrid, padding: int) -> IntArray:
    """
    All max-level cells of a shell ``padding`` finest cells thick around the extent.

    The octree counterpart of the regular grid's padded margin: the extent
    padded by ``padding`` cells on every side, minus the extent itself.

    Args:
        grid: The octree grid.
        padding: Shell thickness in finest cells.

    Returns:
        Cell indices of shape ``(S, 3)``, each outside ``[0, finest_resolution)``
        along at least one axis and inside ``[-padding, finest_resolution + padding)``.
    """
    n = np.array(grid.finest_resolution, dtype=np.int64)
    outer = [np.arange(-padding, n[a] + padding) for a in range(3)]
    inner = [np.arange(n[a]) for a in range(3)]
    sides = [np.r_[-padding:0, n[a]:n[a] + padding] for a in range(3)]

    def block(xs, ys, zs):
        return np.stack(np.meshgrid(xs, ys, zs, indexing="ij"), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3)

    # Slabs outside x (full y, z), then outside y (x inside, full z), then outside z (x, y inside).
    return np.concatenate([
        block(sides[0], outer[1], outer[2]),
        block(inner[0], sides[1], outer[2]),
        block(inner[0], inner[1], sides[2]),
    ]).astype(np.int64)
